pages.text:
foreword
It is truly an honor to receive a request to write a foreword for a book like this, in
this particular space, at this specific time in history, and by an author who I believe
will make significant contributions to this industry during his tenure. That book is
Domain-Specific Small Language Models, the space is generative AI, the time in history is
the tremendous evolutionary acceleration of AI, and the author is Guglielmo Iozzia.
In an era when AI discourse is dominated by ever-larger frontier models and
eye‑catching demos, this book takes a refreshingly pragmatic stance: it is about making
language models actually work for your domain, your data, and your hardware con­
straints. It is written with the practitioner’s learning curve squarely in mind, moving
from foundational concepts to hands‑on experience so that by the time you turn the
last page, you will not only understand why small, domain‑specific language models
matter, you will have run them, tuned them, optimized them, and deployed them on
real‑world infrastructure.
What distinguishes this work is its relentless focus on the realities of distributed and
edge AI. Rather than treating GPUs in the cloud as an infinite resource, the author
leans into the constraints most organizations actually face: tight budgets, on-prem clus­
ters, laptops, and even mobile or embedded devices. From the opening chapters on
the definition and role of small language models (SLMs), it becomes clear that the
goal is not to worship scale, but to show how carefully chosen, well‑tuned models in the
100M to 10B parameter range can deliver outsized business value when pushed as close
as possible to where data is generated and decisions are made. The walkthroughs of
ONNX, quantization techniques, and hardware‑aware optimizations anchor the discus­
sion in concrete practices that materially reduce latency and cost at the edge while pre­
serving useful accuracy.
xii

pages.text:
xiii
foreword
xiii
This is also an excellent grounding text for anyone trying to navigate the LLM-­
versus-SLM decision space with intellectual honesty. The early chapters provide a clear,
hype‑free tour of the Transformer architecture, training paradigms, open source eco­
systems, and the tradeoffs between generalist closed LLMs and domain‑specific models.
From there, the book steadily builds into a toolkit: data preparation, classic fine‑tuning,
PEFT methods such as LoRA, and retrieval‑augmented generation are all presented
with enough depth and runnable code that you can reproduce, adapt, and extend the
examples for your own environment. The result is a rare combination of conceptual
clarity and practical guidance that serves both as an introduction for those new to the
field and as a structured reference for experienced practitioners formalizing their
approach.
Perhaps most compelling is the way the book repeatedly returns to domain reality.
Coding assistants are explored not as abstractions but via end‑to‑end fine‑tuning of
GPT‑2 on Manim code, complete with hyperparameter search and evaluation workflows
that mirror production‑grade ML engineering. Chemistry and life sciences are treated
with equal seriousness, from protein and antibody sequence generation to discussion of
validation workflows and specialized tooling, illustrating how SLMs unlock high‑value
use cases in regulated, data‑sensitive industries. Later chapters connect these capabili­
ties to modern application patterns—RAG pipelines, agentic systems, deployment and
serving patterns, and running on commodity hardware—so that readers finish with a
mental model that spans from theory to architecture to code.
If you are serious about applying generative AI beyond glossy prototypes—especially
in domains where data is sensitive, regulation is strict, or infrastructure is constrained—
this book is worthy of your time. It will not just tell you that small language models are
important; it will show you, step by step, how to build, adapt, and ship them responsibly
in the environments where they matter most.
—Matthew R. Versaggi,
White House Presidential Innovation Fellow in AI, Special cohort of ’24,
former senior director of artificial intelligence and
cognitive technology at Optum Technology/United Healthcare

pages.text:
preface
In early 2022, after finally having the time to complete reading the “Attention is all
you need” paper, I started getting curious about the Transformer architecture and the
potential great use cases in diverse industries (and in life sciences in particular, because
that is the field where I work) for this new kind of neural network. One concern I had
at that time was the concrete risk that such technology could quickly become a prerog­
ative of the large tech organizations that could afford the vast computational resources
necessary to train and execute these models.
Then, inspired by the “run Doom on anything” challenge (a popular trend for soft­
ware engineers to find ways to optimize the source code of that 1993 videogame to run
on any sort of device), I started thinking about ways to optimize small Transformer mod­
els, trained on domain-specific tasks and data, so they could be deployed and executed
in hardware-constrained environments. In June of the same year, I did an ­in-person
­hands-on workshop on this subject at the ODSC Europe conference in London, which
got a lot of interest from ML engineers at the event.
When Manning Publications contacted me a few months later, asking me to write a
book on this topic, I didn’t think twice about accepting. A few weeks after I started writ­
ing the book, OpenAI released the ChatGPT service to the public, powered at that time
by their GPT-3.5 model, and other large tech organizations, such as Google, Anthropic,
and X.AI, soon joined the race to build larger, closed source generalist models to try to
win the consumer market for generative AI.
But the open source community didn’t just watch this happen: lots of initiatives
involving open architectures and weights, and techniques for optimize the training and
execution of language models, started being proposed. It was the right time to write a
book on this topic and provide ML practitioners with a centralized source of informa­
tion about what capabilities are available beyond the commercial offerings, for specific
tasks, and in heavily regulated industries.
xiv

pages.text:
about this book
The focus of this book is on understanding techniques for improving inference per­
formance and costs on pretrained and customized small language models (SLMs)
through optimization and quantization, serving them through diverse API ecosys­
tems, deploying them on diverse hardware (including your own laptop), and integrat­
ing them with other paradigms such as RAG and Agentic AI. All these concepts are
explained in depth and come with complete source code examples. You’ll learn to
minimize the computational horsepower their models require while retaining high–
quality performance times and output.
While a few examples presented in this book describe how to preprocess the data
for training/test, and PEFT (parameter-efficient fine tuning) techniques are also intro­
duced, this book doesn’t focus on training and data-preparation techniques.
Who should read this book
This book is first for ML engineers and data scientists interested in learning how to
manage LLMs in the typical hardware-constrained environment that their company
budget allows for. But it is also for tech leaders motivated to understand how applying
custom language models on corporate data could generate extra business value.
The minimally qualified reader should have the following skills and knowledge:
¡ General understanding of deep learning concepts
¡ Knowledge of the Transformer model’s architecture and internals and the basics
of their training process
¡ Intermediate Python language skills
¡ Hands-on experience with a deep learning framework (PyTorch preferable)

Chapter 1  Small language models
1.1
What are small language models?
Today, regardless of their technical background, most people are familiar with popular
commercial LLMs such as GPT, Claude, and Gemini, which power chatbots and ser­
vices from providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Microsoft. But there’s
still limited awareness of a related category: small language models (SLMs). Like
LLMs, SLMs are designed for natural language processing tasks, but they use fewer
parameters, have a smaller memory footprint, and require less computational power.
That makes them suitable for applications that run on mobile or edge devices or on-­
premises servers or small clusters. SLMs typically range from a few hundred million
to a few billion parameters; there’s no official cutoff, but most stay under 10 billion
parameters. That’s much smaller than LLMs, which often have hundreds of billions of
parameters or more. Because of their small size, SLMs can be optimized for speed and
energy efficiency, which are especially important for on-device or commodity hard­
ware deployments. They can run well on CPUs (when no GPU is available) or on con­
sumer GPUs. Since they run locally, the data can stay local, which is important for tasks
involving sensitive or personal information. Their deployment flexibility also expands
the range of use cases, making them ideal for offline, embedded, and near–real time
applications in areas such as robotics and smart devices (such as mobile phones, lab
equipment, appliances, and manufacturing machinery).
Although SLMs are smaller than LLMs, they aren’t a new type of model. Both are
built on the same core technology—the Transformer architecture and later improve­
ments. The difference is mostly in scale, not the underlying mathematical and architec­
tural principles. As a result, they can address the same kinds of tasks, with SLMs being
optimized more for efficiency than raw power.
NOTE  The Transformer architecture was introduced in the “Attention
is All You Need” paper by Ashish Vaswani and others (https://arxiv.org/
abs/1706.03762).
An important benefit of SLMs is that you can specialize them for specific domains and
tasks at relatively low cost, using domain-specific and private data plus domain knowl­
edge, and apply techniques that don’t require full fine-tuning. Domain-specific tasks
for language models are common in heavily regulated industries where privacy isn’t
optional—healthcare, pharma/biotech, manufacturing, chemistry, finance, and oth­
ers. You’ll see real-world examples in later chapters.

another emerged with the rise of agentic AI and was highlighted in a mid-2025 NVIDIA
research paper: “Small Language Models are the Future of Agentic AI” (https://arxiv
.org/abs/2506.02153). The authors argue that SLMs are powerful enough, better
suited, and more economical for many uses in agentic systems, making them central to
the future of agentic AI. They also suggest that, even when general-purpose conversa­
tion is required, heterogeneous agentic systems—agents that invoke multiple models,

The Transformer architecture
LLMs and SLMs—are the natural choice. The final chapters of this book explore the
relationship between SLMs and agentic AI.
1.2
The Transformer architecture
Before transformers, most tasks on unstructured text were performed using recurrent
neural network (RNN) models. Trained on labeled data, these architectures use their
internal state to process variable-length sequences of text. Later evolutions, such as
LSTM (long short-term memory) or GRU (gated recurrent unit) architectures, intro­
duced the capability to remember and forget important information, but they didn’t
solve one of the major challenges of RNNs: slow training. The data must be processed
sequentially, which limits parallelism across processor cores. The attention mechanism
addressed some RNN limitations by emphasizing relevant parts of the input and down­
playing others, effectively expanding the amount of information the model could
carry forward. Still, it didn’t solve the scalability issues. That required the Transformer
model, which introduced two major changes compared to RNNs:
¡ It uses the self-attention mechanism (a specialization of the attention mechanism
that relates different positions in a sequence to compute a representation of the
sequence itself) so that it can process the entire input all at once.
¡ It has no recurrent structure, so a transformer allows more parallelism than an
RNN, significantly reducing training time.
Transformers didn’t only succeed because of their architecture. Another key com­
ponent is word embeddings—high-dimensional vector representations of words that
capture their semantic and syntactic properties. Embeddings let a Transformer model
manipulate words in a numerical space, where related words end up near one another.
This helps the model treat words as connected, not isolated, entities and understand
how they interact in context.
Transformer architectures have also been proposed for tasks involving other data
types, but multimodal use cases are out of scope for this book, which focuses on genera­
tive models for unstructured text.
The Transformer architecture initially proposed by Google Brain was just the start. As
soon as researchers and professionals started to use it, they quickly found ways to improve
and tailor it for text tasks. The original architecture was encoder–decoder based: the
encoder part converts the input text into a numerical representation, while the decoder
part takes that representation and converts it back to text. Both use an attention mecha­
nism. Over time, it has become clear that some tasks need only the encoder, while others
can rely only on the decoder. This led to two different families of transformers:
¡ BERT (bidirectional encoder representation from transformers) uses only the
encoder part. This kind of architecture performs better on text classification or
prediction tasks.
¡ GPT (generative pretrained transformer) uses only the decoder and generally
performs better on text generation tasks.

Chapter 1  Small language models
Ultimately, your architecture choice will depend on the tasks you want to accomplish.
The examples in this book cover both families.
Another important concept in the Transformer model’s evolution is reinforcement
learning from human feedback (RLHF), a technique used behind the scenes for
OpenAI’s LLMs. As the name suggests, it applies reinforcement learning so an LLM can
learn a policy that maximizes a reward. The models behind ChatGPT are an evolution
of the GPT architecture (the first two versions were open source; later versions moved
to closed source), with RLHF applied for fine-tuning and improved performance.
1.3
Areas of application
The term “LLM” can be misleading. “Large” is clear enough: models range from a few
billion to more than 100 billion parameters, or from tens to hundreds of gigabytes. But
“language” can make people think that these models generate only natural-language
text. Early natural-language processing (NLP) applications did focus on translation
tasks, but newer architectures and capabilities let LLMs handle many tasks beyond
translation:
¡ Language understanding
¡ Text classification
¡ Test generation
¡ Question answering
¡ Document summarization
¡ Semantic parsing
¡ Pattern recognition
¡ Basic math solving
¡ Code generation
¡ Dialogue
¡ General knowledge
¡ Logical inference chains
This makes it possible for an LLM to handle text beyond natural language—anything
that symbolically represents something—as shown in figure 1.1.
LLMs will unlock many real-world use cases across industries.
1.4
The open source revolution
The Transformer architecture didn’t only ignite interest among companies such
as OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google; the open source community also began releas­
ing LLMs under varying licenses for models, code, and training data. Figure 1.2,
taken from a paper titled “A Survey of Large Language Models” (https://arxiv.org/
abs/2303.18223), shows a timeline of the major commercial and open source LLMs
from 2019 to mid-2023 (the paper’s latest update; more models have appeared
since).

1.5
Risks and challenges with generalist LLMs
Commercial, generalist, closed source LLMs from third-party vendors are powerful and
can handle diverse tasks. They can also provide a good experience for non-­technical
users, and you pay only for usage (since you don’t have to manage deployment and
maintenance). But they also come with risks that can outweigh these benefits:
¡ Deployment outside your organization’s network—Any information you include in a
prompt may leave your company and, depending on the usage terms, be used
to fine-tune the model and be exposed to other customers. You’ve likely read
of cases in which employees at large corporations sent sensitive or proprietary
data to external model-hosting services (for example, at Samsung, as discussed in
“Samsung Bans Staff’s AI Use After Spotting ChatGPT Data Leak” [Bloomberg,
May 2, 2023, https://mng.bz/AGEE], and others).
¡ Data leakage risks—Because the model is hosted on infrastructure you don’t con­
trol, a weak cybersecurity posture (unknown to you and hard to mitigate) can
allow malicious actors to access private data. There is evidence that something like
this happened once with ChatGPT (“OpenAI Confirms ChatGPT Data Breach,”
Trend Micro’s blog, May 13, 2023, https://news.trendmicro.com/2023/05/13/
openai-chatgpt-data-breach/).
¡ Model or version drift—A provider can update a model without notice, potentially
changing the behavior and accuracy of applications built on top of it.
¡ Cost unpredictability—Token-based billing can spike, as a provider can decide at
any time to change their subscription prices.
¡ Closeness—You don’t have details about how an LLM was implemented and
trained, so there’s no chance of reproducibility or interpretability, which is often
a requirement in heavily regulated sectors. You also may not see infrastructure or
model-version changes.
¡ Transparency—Data used to train closed source models isn’t publicly disclosed,
so there’s no way to verify whether it’s biased or contains copyrighted data used
without the owner’s permission.
¡ Hallucinations—Generated information may conflict with the source (intrin­
sic hallucination) or be unverifiable from the available source (extrinsic hallu­
cination). Intrinsic hallucinations can occur even in an organization’s models
trained on proprietary data—a challenge with LLMs in general. But extrinsic
hallucinations can’t be mitigated when you don’t have access to, or knowledge
of, the training data.
¡ Compliance—Commercial and closed source LLMs, because of their generalist
nature, don’t follow any sectoral rules.
¡ Harmful content generation—Models can not only reflect societal biases and stereo­
typing but can also produce unsafe content. In the rare cases where a provider

All these risks, plus the fact that large models are trained on many tasks using broad but

1.6
Domain-specific vs. generalist LLMs for business value
Should you move to a custom domain-specific LLM? Several factors can help you make
the right choice.
Generalist pretrained LLMs (both commercial and open source) are largely trained
on content scraped (with or without consent) from the web, drawn from public scien­
tific or code repositories, or taken from human conversations on generic topics. For
tasks that don’t require domain specialization, these models are often powerful enough
to generate useful content that can be reused with little or no refinement. But for spe­
cialized domains and tasks, you’ll need a strategy to tune the pretrained model on
domain-specific data (whether public or private). This process is commonly referred
to as transfer learning. In brief, transfer learning involves taking a model trained on one
task or domain and applying it to a related task or domain.
In heavily regulated domains, there are stricter requirements for staying compliant.
Decisions based on model outcomes cannot cause any sort of harm. In this context, the
availability and quality of domain-specific training data (which you may already have in
house) plays a key role.
Transfer learning does not necessarily involve the full training of a language model.
That’s a possibility, but there are options, as listed in table 1.1.

Another advantage of choosing an open source baseline model is that it will likely
have only a few billion parameters. After tuning it for domain-specific tasks with pri­
vate data, the model will likely remain below 10 billion parameters. From a sustainabil­
ity standpoint, these smaller models generate less CO2 and have less environmental
impact than larger models during training and doing inference.
Finally, let’s look at LLM alignment with users, which you’ve probably heard about.
A common definition of “alignment” in this context is adhering to principles of help­
fulness (following user instructions, completing a task, and providing results), truthful­
ness (providing factual information and acknowledging limitations), and harmlessness
(avoiding biased or toxic responses and refusing to assist with harmful tasks). Commer­
cial closed-source LLM vendors often pursue this by defining what is right and wrong
from their own perspective and then shaping the models accordingly.

In my opinion, alignment should focus less on imposing the provider’s definition of
“right” and more on matching the user’s intent. This is similar to working with a human
collaborator: motives and knowledge/ability are different. Improving knowledge and
ability may lower the mistake rate, but it doesn’t mean the intent is aligned with the per­
son making the request. When you specialize your own models—especially by narrow­
ing the scope to a specific domain—you may have more room to improve this, because
“intent” can take on a domain-specific meaning.

¡ Transformers use self-attention mechanisms to process entire text sequences at
once instead of word by word.
¡ Self-supervised learning creates training labels automatically from text data with­
out human annotation.
¡ BERT models use only the encoder part of transformers for classification and
prediction tasks.
¡ GPT models use only the decoder part of transformers for text-generation tasks.
¡ Word embeddings convert words into numerical vectors that capture semantic
relationships.
¡ RLHF uses reinforcement learning to improve large language model (LLM)
responses based on human feedback.
¡ LLMs can generate any symbolic content including code, math expressions, and
structured data.
¡ Open source LLMs reduce development costs by providing pretrained models as
starting points.
¡ Transfer learning adapts pretrained models to specific domains using
domain-specific data.
¡ Generalist LLMs risk data leakage when they’re deployed outside organizational
networks.
¡ Closed source models lack transparency about training data and model
architecture.
¡ Domain-specific LLMs provide better accuracy for specialized tasks than gener­

¡ Smaller specialized models require less computational power than large gener­

2.1.1
Data preparation for BERT fine-tuning
Let’s consider a classification task using the pretrained bert-base-uncased model
(https://huggingface.co/bert-base-uncased). We first need to gather our data, making
sure each text sample has a class label. Format it as a list of tuples like this:
dataset = [("This movie is a masterpiece!", "Positive"),
    ("Not worth watching!", "Negative"),
    ("Terrific!", "Positive") go here
]
Next, we need to tokenize the training texts, because BERT models work with tokens
rather than raw text.
Notes on tokens
For LLMs, a token is a unit of text the model processes during training and infer­
ence. Tokens can represent words, subwords, characters, punctuation, and special
characters.
How text is tokenized directly affects model performance and language understand­
ing by shaping how well it manages vocabulary, handles out-of-vocabulary words, and
generates coherent responses.
Tokenization is vital in NLP: the token count determines input size and affects pro­
cessing time and memory use. LLMs have a maximum number of tokens they can
accept in a single prompt.
Most pretrained models on the Hugging Face Hub include a custom tokenizer, since
each architecture expects a specific token format. For this example, we’ll use the bert
-base-­uncased tokenizer:
from transformers import BertTokenizer
tokenizer = BertTokenizer.from_pretrained('bert-base-uncased')
For this kind of transformer, special tokens are used to mark the start and end of each
input sequence, and a separator token is used between segments:
max_length = 128
formatted_data = [(f"[CLS] {text} [SEP]", label) for text, label in dataset]
tokenized_data = tokenizer(formatted_data,
               ➥padding=True,
               ➥truncation=True,
               ➥max_length=max_length,
               ➥return_tensors='pt')

2.1.3
Data preparation for RAG
For cases where RAG (discussed in section 2.2) is the best way to specialize a pretrained
language model, you must convert your knowledge base to embeddings and store
them in a vector database. This makes it easy to retrieve information on demand with­
out sacrificing performance or scalability. Many open source and commercial options
are available for this purpose.
In this chapter, we’ll use Facebook AI Similarity Search (FAISS, https://github.com/
facebookresearch/faiss), released as open source under an MIT license and maintained
by Meta Research. FAISS is a library for efficient similarity search and clustering of dense
vectors. It’s implemented in C++ and provides a Python API, so developers don’t need
to worry about implementation details. Used internally at Meta, it supports searches
that are inefficient or impractical with other approaches. It includes nearest-neighbor
implementations for million-to-billion-scale datasets, optimizing the memory/speed/
accuracy tradeoff, and it supports GPUs via the Compute Unified Device Architecture
(CUDA). FAISS offers several similarity-search methods and assumes that instances
are represented as vectors (each identified by an integer) that can be compared using
Euclidean (L2) distance. The most similar vectors to a query vector are those with the
smallest L2 distance.
To get familiar with FAISS, I’ve provided a companion Colab notebook. We’ll walk
through its code in this section. You’ll classify a new input text by calculating its similar­
ity to other text samples in a given category.
In addition to FAISS, we’ll use the sentence-transformers package (https://www
.sbert.net), a framework for sentence, text, and image embeddings.

categorized into three labels: spiderman, ironman, and captainamerica:

relational databases, you’re familiar with a table index: a pointer to data in a table

that embeddings are normalized before being added to the index so they share a
common scale.

2.2
Retrieval-augmented generation
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) integrates data retrieval into LLM content
generation. As shown in figure 2.1, it retrieves relevant data from a larger corpus and
feeds it to a pretrained LLM as an external knowledge base, helping the model pro­
duce more accurate, up-to-date answers.
This is a way to select external information to improve a model’s response. We can
identify two phases:
1	 Retrieval phase—The algorithm searches for and retrieves information based on
the user’s prompt, from private or public data sources, or both.
2	 Content generation phase—After retrieving the relevant embeddings, an LLM uses
the context to generate a natural-language response. The pipeline can also check
the output against the sources to improve transparency and accuracy.

Fine-tuning is similar to pretraining, but it uses a smaller, task-specific, labeled dataset.
To explain the fine-tuning steps, I have provided a companion Colab notebook. This
section walks through the code in that notebook. Note that this section covers the full
fine-tuning of a pretrained LLM (that is, updating all the parameters). In contrast, sec­
tion 2.4 introduces one of the most effective PEFT (parameter-efficient fine-tuning)
techniques, an alternative for adapting a pretrained model to a domain by training only
a small number of parameters; that section also surveys other PEFT methods.
The pretrained LLM in this example is DistilBERT-base, available on the Hugging
Face Hub. It’s a Transformer model that’s smaller and faster than BERT, pretrained
on the same corpus via self-supervised learning, with BERT-base as the teacher. It was
trained on raw text, using an automatic process to generate inputs and labels (no
human labeling), again based on BERT-base. DistilBERT is uncased, meaning it doesn’t
distinguish between uppercase and lowercase letters. In this example, we’ll fine-tune
the model for question answering.
The training dataset must have these three important fields:
¡ question—The question the model should answer
¡ context—The background information from which the model needs to extract
the answer
¡ answers—The starting location of the answer token and the answer text

RAG or fine-tuning?
Which of these two strategies for specializing LLMs should we prefer—RAG or fine-­
tuning? As is often the case, it depends on the specific situation.
RAG is useful when you need up-to-date information (recent data or new data
sources) that wasn’t part of an LLM’s initial training set. It can reduce hallucinations
and improve interpretability because you can trace each answer back to its sources.
RAG is usually less costly than fine-tuning because it requires less labeling and no model
training. But RAG has downsides. In some cases, extra context isn’t enough: if an LLM
struggles with the task it was trained for, additional context won’t help. And at large
data volumes, you also need to account for the infrastructure costs of a vector database
and the implementation and maintenance of data pipelines.
Fine-tuning often outperforms RAG on tasks that require learning complex pat­
terns and relationships, such as drug discovery or code generation. By training on
a task-­specific dataset, an LLM can learn domain nuances, including specialized

accumulation steps. Some ranges were chosen to fit the computational power available

hyperparameters (such as batch size or gradient accumulation steps) may need differ­

which gradients are accumulated before the model’s weights are updated. This
enables a larger effective batch size without exceeding GPU memory limits,
which is especially useful when GPU memory is scarce.

3.4
Domain-specific evaluation
Many statistical metrics can evaluate a language model’s performance at test time. These
metrics provide useful insights for general-domain tasks, especially those based only on
unstructured natural language. But when benchmarking on a specific domain—whether
the model is large, small, or fine-tuned—and the outputs diverge from human language,
you’ll still need a qualitative review by subject matter experts (SMEs) and sometimes also
external strategies and tools. Building on the fine-tuned model for the Manim dataset
we’ve discussed in this chapter, we’ll look at downstream strategies to automate the evalu­
ation of the generated code and reduce the burden on SMEs.
In this case, a complete evaluation pipeline could include the following automated
steps:
¡ Syntax checking—The generated content is Python code, so we must ensure it’s
syntactically valid.
¡ Static analysis for Manim API usage—Parse the generated code to check for
expected Manim classes, methods, or function calls.
¡ After checking that the generated Manim code is syntactically valid, we need to
verify that its execution completes as expected.
¡ Optional—Verify the rendering’s correctness (because Manim output is always an
image or an animation).

import ast
def is_syntax_valid(code_str):
    try:
        ast.parse(code_str)
        return True, ""
    except SyntaxError as e:

NOTE  Python’s ast package (Abstract Syntax Trees, https://docs.python
.org/3/library/ast.html) lets you work with Python’s abstract syntax trees.
We’ll cover it in chapter 7 in the context of Python code generation with
SLMs.
The is_syntax_valid function calls ast.parse and returns True if the generated code
is valid Python syntax, and False otherwise. It checks only syntax, not whether the code
uses a specific API, but it’s a useful first step to catch invalid model responses before
running more complex checks.
The next step is static analysis for the Manim API. It will still use ast, but it will be
tailored to the package being tested. To do that, we can create a dedicated class that
extends the ast module’s NodeVisitor:
from ast import NodeVisitor
class ManimCodeAnalyzer(ast.NodeVisitor):
    def __init__(self):
        self.imports_manim = False
        self.scene_subclass_names = []
        self.play_calls = 0
        self.create_calls = 0
        self.errors = []
This class includes several utility functions that override the parent class’s visit method
and must be named with the visit_ prefix. The first verifies whether the Manim pack­
age is imported directly in the generated code:
def visit_Import(self, node):
    for alias in node.names:
        if alias.name == "manim":
            self.imports_manim = True
    self.generic_visit(node)
Another function will check whether Manim elements are imported via from ... import:
def visit_ImportFrom(self, node):
    if node.module and node.module.startswith("manim"):
        self.imports_manim = True
    self.generic_visit(node)

It also measures similarity between two images. The scikit-image Python
image-processing package (https://scikit-image.org/) provides a ready-to-use
implementation. Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) is a per­
ceptual similarity metric that uses deep-network activations to measure the dis­
tance between image patches. It can also serve as a perceptual loss for image
optimization.

ness in tasks like these:
¡ Sandboxing—Running arbitrary generated code is risky. Use sandboxing tools (for
example, Docker containers or restricted environments) to isolate execution.
¡ Timeouts—Set timeouts to prevent hangs or infinite loops.
¡ Resource limits—Limit CPU, GPU, and memory usage during rendering to save
time and money.

Chapter 3  End-to-end transformer fine-tuning
Summary
¡ GPT-2 small models can be fine-tuned for domain-specific tasks with datasets of a
few hundred samples.
¡ Manim is a Python animation engine for creating mathematical visualizations
with code.
¡ Before tokenizing for language model training, concatenate the instruction and
output fields during preprocessing.
¡ Optuna automates hyperparameter searches and integrates with the Hugging
Face Transformers library.
¡ Model initialization functions create a fresh model instance for each hyperpa­
rameter trial during search.
¡ Training arguments set evaluation strategies, logging intervals, checkpoint sav­
ing, and mixed-precision training.
¡ Early stopping callbacks prevent overfitting by stopping training when the valida­
tion loss stops improving.
¡ Hyperparameter search spaces define ranges for the learning rate, batch size,
weight decay, number of epochs, and other parameters.
¡ You can use Python’s ast module to validate generated code syntax.
¡ Static analysis verifies domain-specific API usage patterns in generated code.
¡ Custom NodeVisitor classes extend ast functionality to analyze framework-­
specific code structures.
¡ Execution testing runs generated code via command-line tools to verify func­
tional correctness.

Chapter 4  Running inference
Our reference open source model is GPT-Neo large (2.7 billion trainable parame­
ters, https://huggingface.co/EleutherAI/gpt-neo-2.7B) from the EleutherAI research
group (https://www.eleuther.ai/). Although GPT-Neo is no longer actively developed
and has been replaced by newer models, it remains a useful example for explaining
the topics in this chapter because it is a Transformer model that replicates the GPT-3
architecture. The topics in this chapter are not limited to GPT-Neo; they apply to any
LLM available through the Hugging Face Transformers and Accelerate (https://
github.com/huggingface/accelerate) libraries (both used in this example) and to
domain-specific models trained on your own data. The code examples in this chapter
are also provided in the two companion Colab notebooks.
4.1.1
Text completion
You can load the GPT-Neo model and its tokenizer the usual way:
import torch
from transformers import GPTNeoForCausalLM, GPT2Tokenizer
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
model_id = "EleutherAI/gpt-neo-2.7B"
tokenizer = GPT2Tokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = GPTNeoForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto")
model.to(device)
The pretrained model (available on the Hugging Face Hub) is loaded onto a GPU to
speed up inference. GPTNeoForCausalLM, a specialized PreTrainedModel class for GPT-
Neo, is available in the Transformers library, and the tokenizer can be downloaded via
the GPT2Tokenizer class. We set device_map to auto so the Accelerate library can run
inference even when the model doesn’t fully fit on the GPU. Accelerate places as many
layers as possible on the fastest devices (here, a single GPU) and offloads the rest to
the CPU—or even disk if RAM is limited. This split is transparent to developers, so the
inference code stays the same. In this example, the model is loaded in float32 type
(the default) because the free-tier Colab GPU can fit it in that format. In other envi­
ronments, you’ll likely need lower precision.
To estimate the memory needed to load a model, Accelerate also provides a
command-­line tool. For GPT-Neo 2.7B, it looks like this:
accelerate estimate-memory EleutherAI/gpt-neo-2.7B
Pass the model ID from the Hugging Face Hub to the command (that’s the only
required argument). The command returns the download size for each available pre­
cision type:
Loading pretrained config for `EleutherAI/gpt-neo-2.7B` from `transformers`...

4.1.2
Few-shot learning
GPT-based models can do more than text completion. Another powerful capability is
few-shot learning: given a few examples in a prompt, the model can generalize to new,
unseen ones. For example, you can use it for few-shot text classification:
prompt = """
Sentence: This movie is very nice.
Sentiment: positive
#####
Sentence: I hated this movie, it sucks.
Sentiment: negative
#####
Sentence: This movie was actually pretty funny.
Sentiment: positive
#####
Sentence: This movie could have been better.
Sentiment: neutral
"""
input_ids = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").input_ids.to(device)
generated_ids = model.generate(input_ids,
                               do_sample=True,
                               temperature=0.9,
                               max_length=200,
                               pad_token_id=50256)
generated_text = tokenizer.decode(generated_ids[0])
Given the initial samples in the prompt, the model starts generating others like them
(and the output includes the input too):

tedious and complex, with challenges that vary by model architecture and the task the
model was trained for.
The Evaluation Harness library (https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation
-­harness) from EleutherAI, also known as LM-Eval, offers a unified way to test LLMs
across many evaluation tasks. It’s implemented in Python and is open source (MIT
license). It includes more than 200 built-in tasks and lets you create custom tasks on
third-party or private data. In addition to its task coverage, it supports several Trans­
former model sources: open source models from the Hugging Face Hub (via the Trans­
formers library), commercial models via the OpenAI API (requires an OpenAI key) and
other providers, models in Neural Magic’s SparseZoo repository (via the DeepSparse
OSS library), and GPTQ-, GGUF-, or GGML-quantized models (covered in chapters 6
and 9).
Depending on the task, different evaluation metrics are supported. Because the
framework is open source and flexible, you can easily extend it and tailor existing tasks.
Task versioning is another key feature, ensuring reproducibility even after tasks are
updated.
LM-Eval isn’t currently available through a Python package installer, so you must
install it from source. Clone the official GitHub repository, and install it with pip
(Python 3.8+ required):
git clone https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness
cd lm-evaluation-harness
pip install -e .
You’re now ready to run evaluation tests. To evaluate a model hosted on the Hugging
Face Hub for a given task, use the provided main.py script:
python main.py \
    --model hf-causal \
    --model_args pretrained=EleutherAI/gpt-neo-2.7B,dtype="float16" \
    --tasks wikitext \
    --device cuda:0
The following options can be set in the script:
¡ model—The model type.
¡ model_args—A list of arguments that specify which model to download from the
Hub and evaluate. Only pretrained is required, and its value must match the
exact Hugging Face Hub model ID. We’ll use GPT-Neo 2.7B throughout this
chapter. You can also pass any other arguments supported by the Transformers
PreTrainedModel class’s from_pretrained method.
¡ tasks—A list of evaluation tasks to run.
¡ device—The device or devices to use (GPU or CPU). Use hardware acceleration
for evaluation tests.

In the preceding example, the evaluation task is wikitext, one of LM-Eval’s built-in
tests. It uses 62 samples from a dataset of verified good and featured Wikipedia articles
(https://huggingface.co/datasets/Salesforce/wikitext) to compute three metrics for
the model under test: word_perplexity (predictive power), byte_perplexity (how well
the model predicts the next byte given prior bytes), and bits_per_byte (average bits
needed to predict the next symbol). LM-Eval can compute additional metrics depend­
ing on the task; see the official GitHub repository for the current list of tasks and met­
rics. For the GPT-Neo model on wikitext, the results are as follows:

4.2
Calculating inference cost
Deploying an LLM to production to handle multiple inference requests costs money.
In the previous section, you learned that larger models cost more because their weights
require more GPU memory, and you often need extra headroom to maintain perfor­
mance. You also saw a CLI tool in the Accelerate library that estimates the required
memory. It’s worth understanding how it makes that calculation so you can estimate
memory needs when serving LLMs outside the Transformers library and make other
sizing decisions. Model documentation for available pretrained open source models
usually lists the number of trainable parameters, but for deployment, you need the
model’s in-memory size so you can decide which GPU (or combination of GPUs) you’ll
need. The formula for estimating inference memory (in GB) is
where
¡ 4 is the number of bytes for each trainable parameter.
¡ P is the model’s total number of trainable parameters (in billions).
¡ F is the number of bits for the chosen precision (32 for FP32, 16 for FP16, 8 for
INT8).
¡ 1.2 is a factor that includes an average 20% overhead due to several factors

Loading the same model in FP16 reduces this to 5.4 GB. If we run the same calculation
for a different model, such as Mistral 7B (https://huggingface.co/mistralai/­Mistral
-7B-v0.3), it requires about 33.6 GB of GPU memory in FP32, or about 16.2 GB in
FP16. Most open source Transformers models are trained in mixed precision (FP16
+ FP32 or BF16 + FP32), which reduces the memory needed for training and, as the
formula shows, for inference too, without a major performance loss when casting an
LLM from FP32 to FP16 (and to INT8, as you’ll see in subsequent chapters). So if you
need to fit within your hardware constraints, it’s fine to load a pretrained model in
FP16.
An LLM’s size is one factor to consider when deciding whether to deploy it to pro­
duction, but it’s not the only one. There are several other important factors:
¡ Full GPU power utilization—Even if GPUs are available in your environment (we’ll
also cover CPU-only setups later), deploying a model and running inference
doesn’t automatically use all GPU resources—or use them efficiently. Techniques
can help you better use the available hardware acceleration.
¡ Time to first token (TTFT)—How quickly does a user see the model’s first output
token after entering a prompt?
¡ Time per output token (TPOT)—How long does it take to generate an output token
for each active user?
¡ Latency—How long does it take to generate a complete response for a user? This
depends on TTFT and TPOT.
¡ Throughput—How many output tokens can the serving system generate per sec­
ond for all users and requests?
Optimization and quantization techniques (the core topic of this book) can reduce
the hardware requirements for LLM serving and help meet latency and throughput
targets. But there are also other challenges, validations, and factors to consider before
and after optimization and quantization. We’ll look at those next.

Areas for improvement (cost savings and performance)
The metrics in the previous section give you a clear picture of how well your LLM’s
inference serving performs, helping you spot areas for improvement that can reduce
costs (use only the computational power you need, get the most from it, and keep users
engaged). Next, we’ll look at what you can do up front to address common inference-­
serving challenges. Although this section uses GPT-Neo as an example, the same con­
siderations apply to other LLM architectures.

Areas for improvement (cost savings and performance)
When choosing a GPU, we focus on three characteristics: compute throughput,
memory, and memory bandwidth. According to the T4’s datasheet, it provides 65
TFLOPS (tera floating-point operations per second) in full (FP32) or half precision
(FP16), 16 GB of memory, and 300 GB/sec of memory bandwidth (that is, up to 300 GB
of data can move from GPU memory to on-chip shared [SRAM] memory per second).
For GPT-Neo, memory isn’t a concern: in half precision it requires 12.96 GB, leaving
room for other inference-time operations.
Using the remaining specs, we can compute the device’s ops/byte ratio, which is the
number of floating-point operations (FLOPS) per second per byte of memory accessed.
We calculate it as follows:
For the T4 GPU, this value is 216.6 ops/byte. To fully use its computational power,
we must perform 216.6 floating-point operations for every byte read from memory.
At runtime, if we observe fewer than 216.6 operations per byte, our system is memory
bound: performance is limited by the data-transfer rate. Conversely, if we need to per­
form more than 216.6 operations per byte but can’t, our system is compute bound:
performance is limited by available compute units, not memory. Our goal is to deter­
mine which case applies on our hardware and optimize accordingly. To do that, we
need to compute the model’s arithmetic intensity: the number of compute operations
divided by the number of bytes accessed. This metric is hardware-agnostic. Next, we
need to identify which model layers demand the most computational power. In Trans­
former architectures, the attention layers are prime candidates because weighting
each next-token prediction based on the relevance of previous tokens is computation­
ally intensive.
Generative Transformer inference sampling has two phases: prefill and autoregres­
sive sampling. In the prefill phase, the model ingests the prompt tokens in parallel
and populates the key–value (KV) cache. This cache stores the model’s state inside the
attention operation. No token generation happens in this phase. In the autoregressive
sampling phase, the model uses the state in the KV cache to sample and decode the
next token. The cache costs storage (GPU VRAM, or CPU RAM when no GPU is avail­
able), but it avoids recomputing attention on all prior tokens at each step. Without the
KV cache, each successive token would take longer to sample because all previously
seen tokens would need to pass through the model again. The generate function in the
Transformers library’s PreTrainedModel classes (encoder-decoder and decoder-only)
exposes a use_cache parameter to enable KV caching; it defaults to True. Still, when
you import third-party code, verify that KV caching is actually enabled—frameworks
other than Transformers may not turn it on by default. Figure 4.1 summarizes how KV
caching works.

4.3.2
Batching
You can also pass an LLM a batch of prompts and generate responses for all of them
at once. We can use static batching (multiple prompts from the same request), or, to
reduce memory-boundedness, we can use dynamic batching: instead of starting genera­
tion immediately for each incoming request, queue requests, and run them together in
a single pass. This reuses model state already loaded in GPU memory across the batch,
increasing arithmetic intensity (more compute per memory access) and making the
workload less memory-bound. The next question is how large the batch can be, which
depends on available GPU memory. In our GPT-Neo example, FP32 precision requires
12.96 GB; on a T4 GPU with 16 GB of VRAM, that leaves 3.04 GB theoretically avail­
able. Let’s calculate how many sequences can fit in that spare memory. We also need to
account for the KV cache. During the prefill phase, the cache is populated with the input
sequence and stores the K and V matrices used in the attention computation. First, we
need the KV-cache size for our case, which we can compute with the following formula:
kv_cache_size = (2 * num_bytes * n_layers * model_dim)
This is measured in bytes/token. In our example, we use 4 bytes (full precision), 24
attention layers, and a model dimension of 2,048. That gives a KV cache size of 393,216
bytes/token (about 0.00039 GB/token), which translates to the following:
kv_cache_tokens
    = 3.04 GB / 0.00039 GB/token
    = 7795 tokens

Areas for improvement (cost savings and performance)
With GPT-Neo’s standard sequence length of 2,048 tokens, our example has enough
capacity to handle a batch of three sequences at once. During inference, batching
three requests to fill the KV cache will increase throughput.
Batching helps in some cases but hurts in others. It’s a good strategy when you’re using
LLMs to process a large document queue asynchronously, because throughput is much
higher than when processing items one by one. You can also schedule inference calls to fill
batches quickly and keep added latency low. But for chatbot-style systems, where latency
must be minimal, batching is usually a poor fit because queuing increases the response
time users feel. In those cases, your main options are to use a GPU with more memory or
better performance, or to use model quantization (covered starting in chapter 5).
4.3.3
Estimating the generation time
Given an LLM and one or more GPUs, it can be useful to estimate up front how long
content generation will take. To do this, we first need to estimate the time to generate
a single token. We can approximate it by dividing the total number of bytes moved by
the GPU’s memory bandwidth:
  time/token = total number of bytes moved/GPU memory bandwidth
You can estimate the number of bytes moved by multiplying the model’s trainable
parameters by the bytes per parameter (based on your chosen precision). For our
GPT-Neo example, the model has 2.7 billion parameters, it’s loaded in full precision
(4 bytes each), and the T4 GPU has 300 GB/s memory bandwidth, so generating a sin­
gle token takes roughly 36 ms.
This isn’t exact: it assumes no on-chip communication during inference, perfect par­
allelism, and no overhead for a forward pass. A more accurate estimate would include
the prefill phase. If we batch all prompt tokens into a single forward pass, a formula for
that metric is shown here:
prefill time = number of tokens * (total number of bytes moved/ GPU compute
bandwidth)
In our GPT-Neo example, assuming 300 tokens and a T4 compute bandwidth of 65
TFLOPS, the prefill time is about 50 ms. Taking this into account, the total generation
time is
total generation time = prefill time + (number of tokens * time/token)
For our example (300 tokens), that’s 50 + (300 × 36) = 10.85 seconds. We can verify if
this estimate is accurate or not:
import time
import numpy as np
prompt = "The story so far: in the beginning, the universe was created."

LLM inference can benefit from techniques such as the following:
¡ Operator fusion—This combines adjacent operators, often improving latency.
¡ Quantization—This compresses an LLM’s weights or activations to use fewer bits.
¡ Compression strategies, such as sparsity (making parts of a model inactive or
zero-valued to reduce computation) or distillation (training a smaller model
using a larger one as a “teacher,” to compress knowledge).
¡ Parallelization—Use tensor parallelism across devices or pipeline parallelism for
larger models.
The rest of the book covers multiple techniques related to quantization, but it also
touches on the other areas listed here.
4.3.4
Optimizing GPU use with DeepSpeed
To reduce compute and memory use—and fit larger models on a single GPU or GPU
cluster—you can use DeepSpeed (https://github.com/microsoft/DeepSpeed). Deep­
Speed is an open source library from Microsoft (Apache 2.0 license) for deep learning
optimization. It makes distributed training and inference easier and more efficient, it
supports PyTorch, and it integrates with Hugging Face’s Transformers and Accelerate
libraries. Key features include ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer, https://arxiv.org/
abs/1910.02054), mixed-precision training, custom model parallelism, and optimiza­
tions for low-latency, high-throughput inference. Model parallelism doesn’t just help
models fit in GPU memory; it can also reduce inference latency for smaller language
models. DeepSpeed also provides inference-specific kernels to further reduce latency

and cost. For compatible Transformer-based models trained with DeepSpeed, Hug­
ging Face, or Megatron, DeepSpeed’s inference mode works without exporting the
model or creating new checkpoints. It automatically partitions the model as needed,
injects high-performance kernels, and manages inter-GPU communication in multi-
GPU environments. This section focuses on inference with DeepSpeed.
Let’s see how DeepSpeed works. For our first example, we’ll again use the GPT-Neo
model, running on a Colab VM with hardware acceleration (a T4 GPU). You can run
Python scripts that use the DeepSpeed API via the deepspeed CLI or programmatically,
which is what we’ll do in this section.
Note that to run inference in Colab or Jupyter notebooks, we’ll need some ini­
tialization code because, at the time of writing, no DeepSpeed launcher is available.
We’ll mock DeepSpeed’s native launcher by setting a few environment variables, as
follows:
import os
os.environ['MASTER_ADDR'] = 'localhost'
os.environ['MASTER_PORT'] = '9999'
os.environ['RANK'] = "0"
os.environ['LOCAL_RANK'] = "0"
os.environ['WORLD_SIZE'] = "1"
The master port can be any available port, and the world size is the number of GPUs.
Rank and world size define the DeepSpeed state; here, we’ll set rank to 0 because we
aren’t using a distributed PyTorch backend.
Now we’ll initialize the DeepSpeed engine and set the default device to CUDA, since
we’ll run inference on an NVIDIA GPU:
import deepspeed
import torch
device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
deepspeed.init_distributed()
ds_device = torch.device(device, int(os.getenv('LOCAL_RANK')))
If you’re not running in a notebook, you can skip the code so far. The rest doesn’t
depend on the execution environment.
Now that the DeepSpeed engine is initialized, we can load the GPT-Neo model the
usual way. For this example, we’ll use half precision to fit both the base model and the
DeepSpeed-optimized version in GPU memory:
import torch
from transformers import GPTNeoForCausalLM, GPT2Tokenizer
model_id = "EleutherAI/gpt-neo-2.7B"
tokenizer = GPT2Tokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)

inject to True to enable inference-kernel injection for our GPT-Neo model. Kernel
injection speeds up deep learning workloads by replacing selected operations (ker­
nels) in the computation graph with DeepSpeed’s optimized versions.

Summary
¡ The GPT-Neo 2.7B model, using the Transformers library, can complete text,
learn from few-shot prompts, and generate code.
¡ Memory requirements are calculated using this formula: memory (GB) = (4 × P)
/ (32 ÷ F) × 1.2, where P is the number of parameters (in billions) and F is the
precision (in bits).
¡ GPT-Neo 2.7B needs 12.96 GB (FP32) or 5.4 GB (FP16); Mistral 7B needs 33.6
GB (FP32) or 16.2 GB (FP16).
¡ Key inference metrics are time to first token (TTFT), time per output token
(TPOT), latency, and throughput.
¡ The KV cache stores attention-layer states to avoid recalculating them for each
token, yielding a 5× speedup in tests.
¡ The operations/byte ratio determines whether a system is memory-bound or
compute-bound; the T4 GPU’s ratio is 216.6 ops/byte.
¡ Arithmetic intensity is operations per byte accessed; GPT-Neo’s 30.29 ops/byte
suggests memory-bound performance.
¡ Dynamic batching processes multiple requests at once, improving throughput by
reusing model weights already in GPU memory.
¡ Batch size is limited by available GPU memory after accounting for model weights
and the KV cache.
¡ Token generation time is estimated by dividing bytes moved by GPU memory
bandwidth; on a T4 GPU, GPT-Neo generates about one token every 36 ms.
¡ The LM-Eval framework standardizes evaluation with 200+ built-in tasks and met­
rics, such as word perplexity, byte perplexity, and bits per byte.
¡ The DeepSpeed library optimizes inference through model parallelism, kernel
injection, and the ZeRO optimizer.
¡ DeepSpeed reduced GPT-Neo inference latency by 18% compared to a baseline
implementation.
¡ The Accelerate library includes the estimate-memory command for calculating
memory requirements across precision levels.

As ML and DL frameworks evolve, portability becomes critical—what we use today may
not be what we’ll use tomorrow. ONNX is a robust open standard that reduces lock-in
to specific frameworks and hardware accelerators, helping ensure an organization’s
models remain usable over time.

was created at Facebook and was soon backed by other companies such as Microsoft,
IBM, Huawei, Intel, AMD, Arm, and Qualcomm. Since then, it has grown into a widely
adopted standard for ML/DL inference. Figure 5.2 lists the companies that currently
support ONNX.
ONNX consists of two projects: the ONNX format and the ONNX runtime. This
section and section 5.2 cover the ONNX format, while sections 5.3 and 5.4 cover the
ONNX runtime.

Besides being cross-framework, ONNX provides APIs for multiple programming lan­
guages. In this book, we’ll use Python (and a little C/C++). Figure 5.3 summarizes all
the possible options with ONNX.
Once you’ve trained a model in a DL framework (or received one from someone
else), you can convert it to ONNX (and optimize it) and then choose from the follow­
ing options:
¡ Executing it directly in the ONNX Runtime (or any other runtime supported by
the framework)
¡ Converting it to another DL framework
¡ Optimizing it further through quantization

final model with any supported runtime. In figure 5.3, the block where the model is

optimizing and quantizing them, and we’ll reference other Python libraries that sup­
port this standard.

ONNX provides a common language that any ML/DL framework can use to describe
its models, making production deployment easier. It also lets you build a unique deploy­
ment pipeline independent of the framework used to create the model. This frame­
work includes a Python runtime for evaluating ONNX models and operators, but use
it with care: it’s intended to clarify ONNX semantics and help with debugging, not for
production—especially when you need high performance.
Regardless of the ML/DL model or framework, building an ONNX graph involves
defining a combination of operators, as described in the next section.

standard matrix operations, reductions, image transformations, deep neural network
layers, and activation functions. Table 5.1 provides a nonexhaustive list of operators rel­
evant to LLMs (see the official ONNX documentation for the complete list).

Operator
Description
Pad
Given a tensor containing the data to be padded, a tensor containing the
number of start and end pad values for axis, and, optionally, a mode and a
constant value, a padded tensor is generated as output.
QuantizeLinear
The linear quantization operator. It consumes a high-precision tensor, a
scale, and a zero point to compute the low-precision/quantized tensor.
Reciprocal
Takes one input tensor and produces one output tensor where the recipro­
cal, y = 1/x, is applied to the tensor element-wise
RegexFullMatch
Performs a full regex match on each element of the input tensor. If an
element fully matches the regex pattern specified as an attribute, the corre­
sponding element in the output is true, and it is false otherwise.
Reshape
Reshapes the input tensor. First input is the data tensor; second input is
a shape tensor which specifies the output shape. It outputs the reshaped
tensor.
Softmax
Computes the normalized exponential values for the given input:
Softmax(input, axis) = Exp(input) / ReduceSum(Exp(input),
axis=axis, keepdims=1)  The axis attribute indicates the dimension
along which Softmax will be performed. The output tensor has the same
shape and contains the Softmax values of the corresponding input.
Transpose
Transposes the input tensor
Unique
Finds the unique elements of a tensor. When an optional attribute axis is
provided, unique subtensors sliced along the axis are returned. Otherwise,
the input tensor is flattened, and unique values of the flattened tensor are
returned.
ONNX is optimized for numerical computation with tensors (multidimensional arrays)
defined by an element type, a shape, and a contiguous array of values. Although ONNX
initially supported only 32-bit floating-point values, later versions added all common
types. You can programmatically list all the supported ONNX types:
import re
from onnx import TensorProto
reg = re.compile('^[0-9A-Z_]+$')
values = {}
for att in sorted(dir(TensorProto)):
    if att in {'DESCRIPTOR'}:
        continue
    if reg.match(att):
        values[getattr(TensorProto, att)] = att
for i, att in sorted(values.items()):
    si = str(i)
    if len(si) == 1:
        si = " " + si
    print("%s: onnx.TensorProto.%s" % (si, att))

To build the graph, we’ll use four functions from the ONNX API:
¡ make_tensor_value_info—Declares an input or output variable with a given
shape and type
¡ make_node—Creates a node from an operation and its inputs and outputs
¡ make_graph—Creates an ONNX graph from the objects created by the previous
two functions
¡ make_model—Merges the graph with additional metadata
ONNX is strongly typed, so you must define the shape and type of each function’s
inputs and outputs. ONNX is built on protobuf (https://github.com/protocolbuffers/
protobuf), a language- and platform-neutral format for serializing structured data.
protobuf provides the definitions needed to describe an ML/DL model; ONNX is
used to serialize and deserialize it. protobuf is responsible for keeping the saved graph
compact.

5.3
The ONNX runtime
The ONNX format defines the ML/DL models converted to this
framework. Another key part of the ecosystem is the ONNX Run­
time (ORT, https://onnxruntime.ai/), which executes ONNX mod­
els efficiently across a wide range of hardware and software platforms
(illustrated earlier in figure 5.1). ORT supports the deployment of
ONNX models on local or cloud servers, as well as on mobile phones
and edge devices, for consistent performance across environments.
When available, ORT uses hardware acceleration for faster inference.
It also includes optimizations such as kernel fusion, quantization,
and layout transformations to speed execution while maintaining
good accuracy. Although ORT supports both training and inference,
it’s most often used for inference, with training left to the original
ML/DL framework. Training with ORT is out of scope for this book.
NOTE  ORT provides bindings for multiple programming lan­
guages; in this book, we’ll use Python.
The inference process follows a fixed set of steps. Once we’ve
trained a model and converted it to ONNX, or implemented one
directly with the ONNX API (such as the linear regression model
in section 5.2), we load it and create an inference session (using
ORT’s InferenceSession class):
Figure 5.4

import onnxruntime as rt
onnx_model_path = "path_to_the_onnx_model"
session = rt.InferenceSession(onnx_model_path)
Next, we prepare the model input (in this example, it will be a NumPy array):
import numpy as np
input_data = np.array([[2.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0]], dtype=np.float32)
We can now run inference:
input_name = session.get_inputs()[0].name
output_name = session.get_outputs()[0].name
result = session.run([output_name], {input_name: input_data})
Finally, we can print the result:
print(f"Output: {result[0]}")

5.4
ONNX runtime providers
To get the most from the underlying hardware on which an ONNX model runs, ORT
uses runtime (execution) providers. These interfaces let you deploy ONNX mod­
els across environments and optimize execution by using each platform’s compute
capabilities. Through a dedicated execution provider, ORT assigns specific nodes or
subgraphs to run on the available hardware, drivers, and related libraries in the deploy­
ment environment. Figure 5.5, from the official ORT documentation, shows how ORT
improves a model’s execution for a given hardware specification.

ONNX runtime providers
At the time of writing, ORT offers many execution providers. Some are production-­
ready; others are preview releases for evaluation. Providers marked as in review are
generally stable and may be suitable for production, but test carefully before deploying
an ONNX model with any provider still labeled as in preview.
Here are ORT’s currently stable execution providers:
¡ Default CPU—Vendor-agnostic CPU.
¡ Intel OpenVINO—Uses the OpenVINO toolkit (https://mng.bz/Jw5p) on CPUs
and GPUs, including edge and mobile devices.
¡ Intel oneDNN—Uses optimized primitives from the Intel Math Kernel Library for
Deep Neural Networks (Intel DNNL). CPU-only.
¡ XNNPACK—Uses XNNPACK (https://github.com/google/XNNPACK), an
optimized floating-point NN inference library for ARM (Android/iOS), Web­
Assembly, and x86.
¡ NVIDIA CUDA—Enables hardware-accelerated computation on CUDA-enabled
NVIDIA GPUs.
¡ NVIDIA TensorRT—Uses NVIDIA’s TensorRT engine (https://developer.nvidia
.com/tensorrt) on supported NVIDIA GPUs.
¡ DirectML—Uses DirectML’s low-level API for ML (https://mng.bz/wZw7); Win­
dows GPUs only.
¡ AMD MIGraphX—AMD’s MiGraphX optimization engine for AMD GPUs
(https://github.com/ROCm/AMDMIGraphX).
¡ AMD ROCm—For AMD GPUs with ROCm (https://mng.bz/qRwK).
¡ Android Neural Networks API—A unified interface to CPUs, GPUs, and neural net­
work accelerators on Android devices (https://mng.bz/7QOx).
¡ Qualcomm QNN—Uses the Qualcomm AI Engine Direct SDK (https://mng.bz/
mZwn) on Qualcomm chipsets.
This is the current list of ORT execution providers still in preview:
¡ TVM—Uses Apache TVM (https://tvm.apache.org/) to optimize models for
CPUs, GPUs, and edge and mobile devices. Currently tested on Linux and Win­
dows, but not on macOS.
¡ ARM Compute Library—Runs inference on Armv8 cores using the Arm Compute
Library engine (https://github.com/ARM-software/ComputeLibrary).
¡ ARM-NN—ArmNN inference engine (https://github.com/ARM-software/
armnn) for Armv8 cores.
¡ CoreML—Uses the Core ML framework (https://developer.apple.com/
machine-learning/core-ml/) to run on Apple’s CPUs, GPUs, and Neural Engine.
¡ Rockchip-NPU—Uses the RKNPU DDK.
¡ Xilinx Vitis-AI—Uses AMD’s development stack for hardware-accelerated AI
inference on AMD platforms.

You can programmatically check the available providers in the destination
environment:
import onnxruntime as rt
rt.get_available_providers()
This returns a Python list. For example, on a system with a CPU and an NVIDIA GPU
(with CUDA drivers installed), the preceding method returns the following:
['CPUExecutionProvider', 'CUDAExecutionProvider']
If multiple providers are available, you can tell ORT the order in which to try them.
Here’s an example:
providers_list = ['CUDAExecutionProvider', 'CPUExecutionProvider']
sess = rt.InferenceSession("model.onnx", providers=providers_list)
Here, we tell ORT to prefer the CUDA provider (when available) over others in the
execution environment.

from onnxruntime.transformers import optimizer
optimized_model_path = os.path.join(output_dir, 'gpt-2-onnx_opt_gpu.onnx')
optimized_model = optimizer.optimize_model(export_model_path,
                                           model_type='gpt2',
                                           use_gpu=True,
                                           num_heads=12,
                                           hidden_size=768)
optimized_model.save_model_to_file(optimized_model_path)
We use the optimizer’s optimize_model method, as in the earlier bert-base-uncased
example. We pass the full path to the converted model, the LLM family type, and the
number of heads and hidden size, and we specify GPU optimization. You can also set
the graph optimization level: 0 (none; the default), 1 (basic), 2 (extended), or 99 (all,
including layout). The same code applies to LLMs with architectures other than GPT-2.
Basic optimization performs constant folding (statically computing parts of the graph
that rely only on constant initializers), removes redundant nodes (such as identity,
slice, unsqueeze, and dropout), and applies semantics-preserving fusions. Extended
optimization applies more complex fusions after graph partitioning, and only to nodes
assigned to the CPU, CUDA, or ROCm (AMD Radeon Open Compute Ecosystem)
execution provider. Layout optimization changes the data layout for applicable nodes
for higher performance; it runs after graph partitioning and only for nodes assigned to
the CPU execution provider.
ONNX optimizations can be done offline or online. The previous code snippet is an
example of offline optimization. Alternatively, you can enable the same optimizations
at inference time by setting the ONNX Runtime session mode, as follows:
import onnxruntime as rt
sess_options = rt.SessionOptions()
sess_options.graph_optimization_level =
➥rt.GraphOptimizationLevel.ORT_ENABLE_EXTENDED
sess_options.optimized_model_filepath = "<model_path\optimized_model.onnx>"
session = rt.InferenceSession(None, sess_options)

In online mode, ONNX Runtime applies all enabled graph optimizations when the
session is initialized, before inference runs. This can increase model startup time
(especially for complex models), which can make it unsuitable for production. In
offline mode, ONNX Runtime applies the optimizations and then serializes the opti­
mized model to disk. Subsequent startups are faster because the model is already
optimized.
5.6.2
I/O binding
Before we move on, consider input and output data when running ONNX models with
execution providers (CPU and GPU). So far, you’ve learned that ONNX models con­
sist of a computation graph implemented as optimized operator kernels for different
hardware, and that ONNX Runtime (ORT) orchestrates execution through execution
providers for a specific target (CPU, GPU, and so on). But what about the data con­
sumed and produced?
By default, ORT places data—regardless of structure (NumPy arrays, dictionaries, or
lists of NumPy arrays)—on the CPU. That’s fine when there’s no hardware acceleration,
but it’s not ideal when a GPU is available and the inference session is configured to run
on the GPU first. In that case, data is copied between CPU and GPU, adding unneces­
sary overhead. ORT provides a custom data structure that supports ONNX data formats
and lets you place data on a device, such as a CUDA-capable GPU. It’s called IOBinding.
With it, input and output data (or just one of them, depending on your configuration)
can be placed on the same device where the ONNX graph runs.
You can configure IOBinding programmatically, as you’ll see next. To keep the
concept simple, we’ll use a small PyTorch model that sums two tensors, but the
same approach applies to more complex models, including LLMs. Let’s define the
model:
import torch
def model():
    class Model(torch.nn.Module):
        def __init__(self):
            super(Model, self).__init__()
        def forward(self, x, y):
            return x.add(y)
    return Model()
Now let’s convert it to ONNX programmatically:
MODEL_FILE = '.model.onnx'
type = torch.float32
sample_x = torch.ones(3, dtype=type)
sample_y = torch.zeros(3, dtype=type)

a result, FP32 became the standard for deep-learning training.
In floating-point numbers, bits are the binary digits used to store a value in a com­
puter’s memory. More bits mean higher precision and a wider representable range. A
floating-point value has three parts: the sign, the exponent, and the mantissa. In 32-bit
floating point, 1 bit is for the sign, 8 bits are for the exponent, and 23 bits are for the
mantissa (see figure 6.1).

DL models are generally robust to lower­
precision arithmetic. In most cases, the
small loss of precision from using 32-bit
floats instead of 64-bit floats doesn’t notice­
ably affect predictive performance, so the
tradeoff is worth it. But moving to 16-bit
precision can be trickier. That’s why mixed-precision training is used instead of pure
16-bit training. With mixed precision, only some parameters and operations use 16-bit
floats, switching between 16-bit and 32-bit during training. The typical workflow is to
convert weights to lower precision for faster computation, compute gradients in lower
precision, convert gradients back to higher precision for numerical stability, and then
update the original weights using scaled gradients.
So far, we’ve focused on training. What about inference? If you train the same LLM
in FP32 and FP16, memory use is roughly half for the latter (as expected), but perfor­
mance can degrade significantly. With mixed precision (FP16 + FP32), memory use is
higher than with pure FP16 but still lower than pure FP32, while performance is compa­
rable, and often slightly better. This may sound odd, but lower precision can introduce
noise during training that improves generalization and reduces overfitting, potentially
increasing accuracy.
Another floating-point format has been
introduced recently and is increasingly
used: brain floating point (BF16), devel­
oped by Google for ML/DL on tensor pro­
cessing units (TPUs). Compared to F16 (see
figure 6.3), it extends dynamic range at the
cost of lower precision.

BF16 uses 1 bit for the sign, 8 for the
exponent, and 7 for the mantissa. This
lower precision may affect the accuracy of
some calculations, but in most deep learn­
ing applications, it has minimal effect on model performance. Models trained in BF16
typically deliver comparable inference performance and memory use to those trained

6.2
8-bit quantization
In scenarios with tight computational power constraints, or when deploying to small
devices, LLMs can be too large and too slow for inference. Using reduced precision
(FP16) alone may not make a model fit the target hardware. Two common solutions
are knowledge distillation and quantization, both of which reduce model size with lim­
ited performance loss. Knowledge distillation trains a smaller model to mimic a larger
one—this can happen by transferring knowledge from the larger to the smaller model.
For hardware-specific deployment, quantization is often the better choice, and recent
advances in stable quantization have made it preferable to distillation in many cases.
This book focuses on quantization to simplify LLM deployment and improve perfor­
mance across a wide range of hardware.
Quantization reduces numeric precision: lowering the bit width of an LLM’s weights
and activations shrinks the model and can speed up inference. By using lower-precision
types, such as 8-bit integers, you reduce the memory footprint at the cost of quantiza­
tion error. For example, 8-bit values can pack about four times as many numbers as
32-bit floats in the same amount of memory. The goal is to balance precision against
memory use (and speed).
There are two types of quantization: post-training quantization (PTQ), applied after
training, and quantization-aware training (QAT), done during training. This book
focuses mostly on PTQ, because starting from a pretrained LLM baseline typically
doesn’t require full training—only fine-tuning, PEFT, or RAG to adapt it to a specific
domain.
How does 8-bit quantization work in practice? Let’s walk through a numerical
example. There are several quantization schemes; the most common are zero-point and
absmax. Suppose we want to convert an FP32 tensor to INT8. With zero-point quantiza­
tion, we assume an asymmetric input distribution, so we scale by the INT8 value range
(255) divided by the difference between the input’s maximum and minimum values

We can convert all model layers to INT8 format and then quantize the full model

import torch
def absmax_quantize(X):
    scale = 127 / torch.max(torch.abs(X))
    X_quant = (scale * X).round()
    X_dequant = X_quant / scale
    return X_quant.to(torch.int8), X_dequant
As described earlier in section 6.2, it runs three steps: calculate the scale, quantize to
INT8, and dequantize back to FP32. For a given input, it returns both the quantized
and dequantized values. Let’s use it to quantize all the GPT-2 model weights:

for param in model_abs.parameters():
    _, dequantized = absmax_quantize(param.data)
    param.data = dequantized
    weights_abs.append(dequantized)

def calculate_perplexity(model, text, device):
    encodings = tokenizer(text, return_tensors='pt').to(device)
    input_ids = encodings.input_ids
    target_ids = input_ids.clone()
    with torch.no_grad():
        outputs = model(input_ids, labels=target_ids)
    neg_log_likelihood = outputs.loss
    perplexity = torch.exp(neg_log_likelihood)
    return perplexity
This function expects three arguments: a model, a text prompt, and the device to off­
load the model weights to. It encodes the input sequence, prepares the model inputs,
generates text, computes the loss, and uses it to calculate the perplexity score (which
is returned to the caller). We can apply this function to both models—the original and
the absmax-quantized one—using as the prompt the text each model generated a few
steps earlier:
perplexity = calculate_perplexity(model, original_text, device)
perplexity_absmax = calculate_perplexity(model_abs, absmax_text, device)

single run isn’t very reliable; you should repeat the experiment several times to under­
stand the differences between the models. This is easier if you first create two reusable

6.2.2
LLM.int8() and quantization
In the previous example, for simplicity, we applied per-tensor quantization to all the
model layers. But you can quantize at different granularities. Quantizing the whole
model in one pass can seriously degrade performance, but quantizing individual val­
ues creates too much overhead. In practice, a good compromise is vector-wise quan­
tization, which accounts for variability across rows and columns within a tensor. This
is often sufficient for domain-specific models, since they’re typically under 7 billion
parameters. Above that threshold, you may see outlier features in any LLM layer. Even
a single outlier can significantly reduce precision for the other values, and you can’t
just discard outliers without a nontrivial hit to model performance.
