What can we do instead? Fortunately, there’s no need for custom implementations—
LLM.int8() already addresses this. First introduced in a 2022 paper (https://arxiv.org/
abs/2208.07339), it enables INT8 matrix multiplication for LLMs with no accuracy
loss. It cuts inference memory roughly in half while retaining full-precision perfor­
mance. It uses an absmax quantization scheme with mixed precision: outlier features
are processed in FP16 to preserve accuracy, while the remaining values use INT8. This
approach reduces an LLM’s memory footprint by nearly two times.
LLM.int8() performs matrix multiplication in three steps:
1	 It extracts columns with outlier features (a small number of weights or activations
whose values are much larger in magnitude than the rest of the distribution)
from the input hidden states using a custom threshold.
2	 Then it multiplies the outliers in FP16 and the rest in INT8 using vector-wise
quantization.
3	 Finally, it dequantizes the non-outlier results (INT8 to FP16), adds them to the
outlier results, and produces the full FP16 result.
There’s more good news: LLM.int8() is integrated into the Hugging Face Transformers
API. It requires the Accelerate and bitsandbytes (https://github.com/bitsandbytes
-foundation/bitsandbytes) libraries; bitsandbytes implements LLM.int8() quantization
and runs on GPUs only.
A companion Colab notebook contains the full source code for this section and
requires GPU acceleration. The steps are similar to those in section 6.2.1, so only the
main parts are discussed here.

the Transformers auto class:

                                             device_map='auto',

                                             )

we can plot the weight distributions for the original and quantized models to see how

The high-level approach uses Optimum (https://github.com/huggingface/

We now need to quantize the model to 8-bit precision, using dynamic quantization.
Unlike static quantization, dynamic quantization runs only on the CPU, not the GPU.
That’s not a problem, because quantization happens offline, and inference is still fast
without hardware acceleration (as you’ll see later in this section).
We’ll create an instance of ORTQuantizer (Optimum’s class for ONNX Runtime
quantization of models shared on the Hub) and define the quantization configuration.
Then we can apply it to the original model:
from optimum.onnxruntime import ORTQuantizer
from optimum.onnxruntime.configuration import AutoQuantizationConfig

                                              per_channel=False)
model_quantized_path = dynamic_quantizer.quantize(
    save_dir=onnx_path,
    quantization_config=dqconfig,
)

According to the Hugging Face Hub, the original model’s accuracy is 92.5%. Running
the preceding code yields 92.34% for the quantized model (99.82% of the FP32 base­
line), a negligible loss. But what about latency? We can write a quick-and-dirty bench­
mark function to compare the two versions (chapters 7 and 10 show better ONNX
benchmarking approaches):
def measure_latency(payload_prompt, pipe):
    latencies = []
    for _ in range(10):
        _ = pipe(payload_prompt)
    for _ in range(300):
        start_time = perf_counter()
        _ =  pipe(payload_prompt)
        latency = perf_counter() - start_time
        latencies.append(latency)
    time_avg_ms = 1000 * np.mean(latencies)
    time_std_ms = 1000 * np.std(latencies)
    time_p95_ms = 1000 * np.percentile(latencies,95)
    return f"P95 latency (ms) - {time_p95_ms}; Average latency (ms)
➥ - {time_avg_ms:.2f} +\- {time_std_ms:.2f};", time_p95_ms
This pipeline runs a short warmup (a few initial inference passes to stabilize caches
and compilation effects), benchmarks a set number of steps, then reports the average
latency and standard deviation. Running it on both the original and quantized model
pipelines with a 142-token prompt shows a 1.86x inference speedup with the quantized
model. With comparable performance, quantization significantly reduces latency.

6.4
4-bit quantization
In the previous section, you saw practical examples of LLM quantization from single
precision to 8-bit integer format. Now let’s push further and reduce the model size by
quantizing to a lower precision, such as 4-bit integers.
6.4.1
4-bit quantization with GPTQ
After 8-bit quantization proved effective at shrinking LLMs with little loss in accuracy,
new techniques emerged for 4-bit integer quantization. The first was GPTQ, proposed
in 2022 in “GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-Trained
Transformers” (https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323). GPTQ is a one-shot weight-­
quantization method based on approximate second-order information that is both
accurate and efficient. It can reduce GPT-based models to 3 or 4 bits per weight with
negligible accuracy loss compared to the uncompressed baseline. The paper reports
that even 175B-parameter models can run inference on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU
after quantization, and the method can also yield strong results on smaller models
and less powerful GPUs. The paper covers the math and methodology, but you don’t
need to master them to use GPTQ because a solid Python implementation is available
and integrated into major LLM libraries. The de facto standard implementation is the
AutoGPTQ package (https://github.com/AutoGPTQ/AutoGPTQ). Consult the asso­
ciated repository only if you want low-level implementation details—AutoGPTQ is also
integrated into the Hugging Face Transformers, Optimum, and PEFT libraries. In this
chapter, we’ll use the original implementation to make it easier to see how 4-bit quanti­
zation works (higher-level APIs hide many details).
In this section, you’ll learn how to use AutoGPTQ. A companion Colab notebook pro­
vides the full source code for the example. Along with AutoGPTQ, we’ll use the Hug­
ging Face Transformers library to apply 4-bit quantization to the GPT-2 XL model (1.5B
parameters, https://huggingface.co/openai-community/gpt2-xl). We’ll run with hard­
ware acceleration on a single NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU.

your PyTorch and CUDA driver versions), we can start implementing the model quanti­

Apple Silicon, ggml-quantized models can also run on x86 (using AVX/AVX2 intrin­
sics), ppc64 (using VSX intrinsics), and Android. ggml is fast in part because it has no
third-party dependencies and does zero memory allocations at runtime.
ggml can also quantize other Transformer architectures (for example, image and
audio models), but in this chapter (and the next) we focus on LLMs and how to run
them efficiently on CPUs. GPTQ inference is optimized for GPUs, whereas ggml infer­
ence is optimized for CPUs, which makes it practical for many environments, including
typical laptops and personal computers. Recent releases also support limited GPU off­
loading at inference time—not to speed up inference, but to reduce power use and free
up CPU resources.
Later chapters return to ggml for more advanced optimization and quantization
techniques; unlike Hugging Face’s Python libraries, it requires more low-level program­
ming knowledge.
Scripts for converting some of the most popular open source LLMs to GGML format
are available in ggml’s official GitHub repository, and many quantized versions are
already available for download from the Hugging Face Hub. Although ggml is written in
C, you can load quantized models and run inference entirely in Python using Hugging
Face Transformers and CTransformers (https://github.com/marella/ctransformers).
CTransformers provides Python bindings for Transformer models implemented in
C/C++ via ggml.

Hugging Face Transformers pipeline API:

Summary
¡ Floating-point precision affects memory use and computational speed in lan­
guage model operations.

see how to optimize and, if needed, quantize them to run inference on commodity hard­
ware (ideally on our laptops) while maintaining good performance. First, though, we’ll
consider the present and future of human programmers in this era of coding assistants.
Given the availability of commercial and open-source copilots, many CEOs and other
executives have predicted the obsolescence of programmers in favor of prompt engi­
neers, or claimed that everyone (whatever their background) will become a software
architect. How true is that? Let’s start with large generalist models. Several research
efforts, such as SWE-bench (https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770), evaluate large com­
mercial models such as GPT-4 and Claude 2 on real-world programming challenges
based on real code. The paper focuses on Python (2,294 issues and related pull requests
from GitHub repositories), but many benchmarks for other languages can be found
online. Neither model scored well on these problems, even with knowledge retrieval.
More prompt engineering helps little: even with a larger context, results can still be con­
fused or random, at the cost of more processing power and the user’s time. Since the
paper’s publication, many large and small models, with or without retrieval-­augmented
generation (RAG), have been benchmarked. The updated leaderboard is available at
https://www.swebench.com/ (updated every Monday). Over time, new models and
supporting techniques have improved results, but none of the benchmarked models
can yet be used without expert human supervision (see figure 7.1).

Generating Python code with a Transformer architecture
Several factors explain the modest performance. Resolving software engineering prob­
lems often requires coordinating changes across multiple functions, classes, and files,
interacting with execution environments, and reasoning well beyond straightforward
code generation. These are areas where humans still outperform ML models. And
because these models are trained as generalists, they rarely match the depth of exper­
tise that professional software engineers bring to complex programming tasks.
Dedicated models for programming tasks, such as Microsoft Copilot, are often more
accurate and can handle more complex work than general-purpose models. Still, they
can be costly for some organizations and require human oversight and guardrails to
prevent data leakage. They may also lack transparency about where their training data
comes from. These tools raise the same privacy, IP, and safety concerns discussed earlier
in this book, especially when they rely on large, closed models.
Luckily for us, LLMs specialized for this kind of task are available, and specialization
drastically reduces model size. We can see this in the industry’s growing move toward
smaller, more focused coding LLMs that, despite having only a few billion parameters,
match, and sometimes outperform, larger models on evaluation benchmarks. This isn’t
surprising: if the main task is coding in one or a few programming languages, you can
remove much of the irrelevant knowledge in large generalist models. A smaller, more
focused data pool is easier to keep relevant, cheaper to train, and less likely to inadver­
tently include copyrighted or unauthorized data.
Back to the main question: Will generative AI replace human programmers? Prob­
ably not, even if models reach 98% to 100% accuracy on coding tasks. Coding is only
one part of software development. It also involves investing in new things, understand­
ing users’ requirements and needs, translating ideas into something buildable, and
polishing the result. These steps require human judgment and cannot be reduced
to next-token generation. In my opinion, software engineers will not shift into roles
focused mainly on reviewing and verifying AI-generated code, even if generative mod­
els become highly accurate. These models can still be a big help, and I wouldn’t dis­
courage professionals from using them. But domain knowledge is always needed to
use them well: a good software engineer can become a better software engineer using a
code assistant, but someone with little or no software engineering knowledge will not.
Software engineering isn’t different from other domains when it comes to support from
AI-based assistants.

CodeGen is conceptually comparable to OpenAI’s Codex, the model that was behind
GitHub Copilot when Salesforce released its own proposal. It offers two families of pre­
trained models: multi, trained to generate code in six languages (C, C++, Go, Java, JavaS­
cript, and Python), and mono, trained to generate Python only. Each family includes
four sizes: 350M (350 million parameters), 2B (2.7 billion parameters), 6B (6.1 billion
parameters), and 16B (16.1 billion parameters). To show CodeGen’s scale at release,
figure 7.2 compares the largest model with other open or closed source LLMs for the

tokens and 0.9 s for requests that generate 50 to 250 tokens. Still, the 350M model isn’t suit­
able for production; later in this chapter, we’ll discuss the quality of the generated results.

The 2B model is a more robust candidate (as are the larger versions). This model
family can generate code that uses not only Python’s standard library but also third-
party open source libraries. Even so, the 350M version is a good choice for explaining
the concepts covered in this chapter.
The first Colab notebook for this chapter contains a complete, end-to-end example
of optimizing inference for CodeGen 350M mono. We’ll use this smaller model to show
that even a few hundred million–parameter model leaves room for inference optimiza­
tion, and the same ideas apply to the larger mono models.
All the CodeGen checkpoints (mono and multi) are available on the Hugging Face
Hub and via the Transformers library, so we can download the pretrained model and its
tokenizer as usual:
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, CodeGenForCausalLM
device = "cpu"
model_id = "Salesforce/codegen-350M-mono"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = CodeGenForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id).to(device)
model.eval()
The only difference here is the use of CodeGenForCausalLM, Hugging Face Transform­
ers’ auto class for CodeGen models.
This example doesn’t require hardware acceleration. We’ll assume the model and
data are loaded and running on CPUs. The small CodeGen mono model works as
follows:
prompt = "def hello_world():"
input_ids = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").input_ids
generated_ids = model.generate(input_ids, max_length=12)
print(tokenizer.decode(generated_ids[0],
                       skip_special_tokens=True,
                       pad_token_id=50256))
Given a prompt with a descriptively named function definition, it generates the func­
tion body as follows:
def hello_world():
    print("Hello World")
This is one way to prompt the CodeGen models. It’s the only approach that works well
for the 350M model, though others are possible. With the 2B and larger CodeGen

from contextlib import contextmanager
from time import perf_counter
@contextmanager
def track_infer_time(time_buffer):
    start_time = perf_counter()
    yield
    end_time = perf_counter()
    time_buffer.append(end_time - start_time)
The second utility is the BenchmarkInferenceResult class, used to collect metrics across
benchmarks:
from dataclasses import dataclass
@dataclass
class BenchmarkInferenceResult:
    model_inference_time: [int]
    optimized_model_path: str
The benchmark code for the vanilla CodeGen model is then quite simple:
from tqdm import trange

    ("cpu", "PyTorch CPU"),

    time_buffer = []
    for _ in trange(inference_runs, desc=f"Tracking

7.2.3
Model evaluation
Several open source Python packages, such as Hugging Face’s Evaluate and EleutherAI’s
LLM Evaluation Harness (discussed in chapters 6 and 4, respectively), plus public
datasets, are available for LLM evaluation. But generating unstructured outputs such as
Python (or other) code calls for extra choices to make evaluation robust and meaningful.
In this section, we’ll walk through an approach based on the CodeGen 350M
mono model and its ONNX-converted, 8-bit-quantized variants introduced in sec­
tion 7.2.1, and which you can also apply to other LLMs specialized on Python code
generation. The code comes from Amazon Science’s ReCode paper (https://arxiv
.org/abs/2212.10264) and is shared in a Colab notebook for this chapter. I chose this
approach because ReCode defines robustness metrics for code generation models by
measuring worst-case behavior under different prompt perturbations (language mod­
els are sensitive to prompt changes). This provides a practical way to assess code quality
for production use.
We’ll use OpenAI’s HumanEval evaluation dataset (https://github.com/openai/
human-eval), introduced in “Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code”
(https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03374). HumanEval is also available on the Hugging Face
Hub (https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/openai_humaneval). It contains 164
Python programming problems, each with a function signature, docstring, body, and
several unit tests. The comments and docstrings are in English. The dataset fields are as
follows:
¡ task_id—The identifier of the data sample
¡ prompt—The input for the model, containing function header and docstrings
¡ canonical_solution—A code solution for the problem in the prompt
¡ test—A test function to validate the generated code for correctness
¡ entry_point—The starting point for the tests
You can download this dataset via the Hugging Face Datasets API and then transform
it into the format expected by the ReCode evaluation. Alternatively, you can download
a ready-to-use JSON copy from the ReCode GitHub repo:

7.2.4
Python code generation with better models
When Salesforce released version 2.0 of the CodeGen models, it again offered the
mono and multi families in four sizes each, roughly matching the first-generation
sizes.
The latest generation is CodeGen 2.5, which comes in a single size—7 billion param­
eters for both the mono and multi versions. It features robust infill sampling (it can
read text on both the left and right side of the current position), and it is optimized
for fast sampling with FlashAttention, making it suitable for efficient serving and local
deployment, including on personal machines. FlashAttention is an alternative to tradi­
tional self-attention that makes LLMs more efficient, enabling faster training and infer­
ence. Instead of repeatedly reading and writing keys, queries, and values from GPU
HBM (large but relatively slow), it loads them once into SRAM (smaller but faster),
fuses the attention operations, and then writes the results back.
All the CodeGen 1 and 2 models were released under the permissive Apache 2.0
license, and CodeGen 2.5 multi and mono use the same license. Note that the Code­
Gen 2.5 instruct model is available for research only, not for commercial use.
Generating Python code with the CodeGen 2.5 mono model works the same way as
with the CodeGen 1 mono model discussed earlier in this chapter. First, download the
model and tokenizer from the Hugging Face Hub:

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained model_id)
You can then generate code by invoking the generate method on the tokenized prompt:
text = "def hello_world():"
input_ids = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt").input_ids
generated_ids = model.generate(input_ids, max_length=128)
print(tokenizer.decode(generated_ids[0], skip_special_tokens=True)

As mentioned earlier, CodeGen 2.5 also works well for code infilling—filling in missing
parts of an incomplete code snippet. It requires the prompt to follow this formatting
convention:
¡ Insert a <mask_1> token at the cursor.
¡ Add a <sep> token to mark the boundary.
¡ Insert another <mask_1> token to specify which mask to infill.
Here’s an example:
def format(prefix, suffix):
  return prefix + "<mask_1>" + suffix + "<|endoftext|>"
  ➥+ "<sep>" + "<mask_1>"
Then generate the body of a Python function, as in the following example:
prefix = "def hello_world():\n    "
suffix = "    return greeting_message"
We need to format the prompt with our custom format function, tokenize it, and then
invoke the model’s generate method:
text = format(prefix, suffix)
input_ids = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt").input_ids
generated_ids = model.generate(input_ids, max_length=128)
print(tokenizer.decode(generated_ids[0],
➥ skip_special_tokens=False)[len(text):])
Other small language models for code generation have been proposed. One strong
example is StarCoder2 (https://huggingface.co/bigcode/starcoder2-3b), a 3 billion–
parameter model developed by BigCode, an open scientific collaboration focused on
the responsible development and use of large language models for code, supported by
ServiceNow, Hugging Face, and NVIDIA. Introduced in a 2024 paper (https://arxiv
.org/abs/2402.19173), it was trained on 3+ trillion tokens from the Stack v2 dataset
(https://huggingface.co/datasets/bigcode/the-stack-v2), covering code in 17 pro­
gramming languages (including Python) plus curated natural language text from Wiki­
pedia, arXiv, and GitHub issues. StarCoder2 uses grouped-query attention (proposed
in a 2023 paper; https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245v3) to speed inference, and it has a
16,384-token context window with a 4,096-token sliding-window attention. Because it is
not instruction-tuned, it is best suited to generating a function body when the function
header is specified in the prompt, but the official GitHub repo (https://github.com/
bigcode-project/starcoder2) includes tuning scripts.

7.3
Coding assistance on commodity hardware
The CodeGen and StarCoder models discussed in section 7.2 showed good inference
performance (with room for further optimization), making them suitable for deploy­
ment behind an API to enable code generation from client applications. It would also
be useful to have one of these models running smoothly on a laptop as a coding assis­
tant. In this section, we’ll verify an optimized small language model to run locally as a
code assistant with acceptable performance. Our target laptop is a MacBook Air with
an Apple M1 chip and 8 GB of unified memory. I chose one of the less powerful Apple
M-series laptops to make things more challenging and to show that, even with this
hardware, you can optimize inference and run useful, domain-specific SLMs smoothly.
Our reference model will be StarCoder v2 3B.
If you browse the Hugging Face Hub, you’ll find several LLMs (including StarCoder
v2 3B) already available in GGUF format. A natural way to try one of these quantized
models for laptop inference is to use the Transformers API, just as you would with a
standard FP32 or FP16 model:
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM
model_id = "second-state/StarCoder2-3B-GGUF"
filename = "starcoder2-3b-Q2_K.gguf"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id, gguf_file=filename)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, gguf_file=filename)
The only difference here is the filename of the quantized model checkpoint to down­
load. GGUF offers multiple quantization options, so several quantized versions of the
same model may be available.
Although the Hugging Face Hub can host GGUF models, and the Transformers
library can download them, Transformers still can’t use models in quantized GGUF for­
mat. After a GGUF download completes, the model is automatically unquantized, and
inference can run only in the original format. That puts us back at the start, because the
original model is typically too large to run locally with limited CPU/GPU and memory.

Coding assistance on commodity hardware
The only workaround, if we want to go through the Transformers API, is to save the
model to disk after downloading:
model_checkpoint_dir = 'starcoderv2-checkpoint-dir'
tokenizer.save_pretrained(model_checkpoint_dir)
model.save_pretrained(model_checkpoint_dir)
We can then apply a quantization technique to it.
But there are smarter options. llama.cpp (https://github.com/ggerganov/llama
.cpp) is an open source C/C++ library and project that enables inference for several
LLMs on a wide range of hardware, including devices without a GPU (such as laptops
and mobile phones). GGUF is the binary file format used by llama.cpp.
To keep things simple, we will use llama-cpp-python (https://github.com/abetlen/
llama-cpp-python), which provides Python bindings for llama.cpp and supports Apple’s
Metal (MPS, Metal Performance Shaders) backend. To install it, you need Python 3.8+
and a C compiler for your machine (for example, Xcode on macOS). After creating a
virtual environment, you can install llama-cpp-python from PyPI:
CMAKE_ARGS="-DGGML_METAL=on" pip install llama-cpp-python
The preceding command builds and installs the library, including building and install­
ing llama.cpp. You’ll also need the huggingface-hub library to download the model:
!pip install huggingface-hub
Now that everything is set up, we can start coding to make the model available for local
inference. First, we’ll import the required dependencies:
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from llama_cpp import Llama
Then we can download the model from the Hugging Face Hub:
model_name = "second-state/StarCoder2-3B-GGUF "
model_file = "starcoder2-3b-Q4_K_M.gguf "
model_path = hf_hub_download(model_name, filename=model_file)
The GGUF-converted model used in this example is Second State’s 4-bit K_M-quantized
version of StarCoder v2 3B (https://huggingface.co/second-state/StarCoder2-3B
-GGUF). After downloading it to your laptop, you can load it into memory using the
llama-cpp-python library’s Llama class, as follows:
llm = Llama(
    model_path=model_path,
    n_ctx=3072,
    n_threads=4
    n_gpu_layers=0
)

Chapter 7  Generating Python code
We’ve specified the local path to the model checkpoints, the context size (3,072 for
StarCoder v2 3B), the number of CPU cores to use, and how many model layers to
offload to the GPU (none in this example, since we want to run inference on the CPU
only).
Next, we can set arguments for code generation, such as the maximum number of
new tokens, a stop policy, whether to echo the prompt in the output, the decoding strat­
egy, and other inference options:
generation_kwargs = {
    "max_tokens":20,
    "stop":["</s>"],
    "echo":False,
    "top_k":1
}
Now we can set a prompt and run inference:
prompt = "def hello_world():"
res = llm(prompt, **generation_kwargs)
The preceding command outputs a dictionary in an OpenAI-compatible format:
{
  "id": "cmpl-xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx",
  "object": "text_completion",
  "created": xxxxxxxxxx,
  "model": "./models/starcoder2-3b-Q4_K_M.gguf",
  "choices": [
    {
      "text": "\n    return 'Hello World!\n\n",
      "index": 0,
      "logprobs": None,
      "finish_reason": "length"
    }
  ],
  "usage": {
    "prompt_tokens": 5,
    "completion_tokens": 20,
    "total_tokens": 25
  }
}
To return only the generated text and omit the other response fields, use this
command:
print(res["choices"][0]["text"])
The first time you run this code, it will be slower because it must download the model
checkpoints locally. After that first run, you can generate code completely offline.

Summary
You can benchmark this local model’s performance the same way you did for the
CodeGen models. Repeat the inference tests with the same configuration used for the
smaller models, and you’ll see latency and throughput results like the following:
             GGUF 4-bit K_M
Average_latency (ms) 432.545684
Latency_P50          432.409188
Latency_P75          436.077177
Latency_P90          438.191962
Latency_P95          438.622171
Latency_P99          440.215217
Throughput               2.311895
The overall performance (using only four threads and no GPU) is comparable to the
4-bit quantized CodeGen model, which is acceptable for local use. You can evaluate the
generated code as explained in section 7.2.3.
So far, we’ve run inference from the CLI by executing a Python script with a prompt.
You can also run in chat mode (llama-cpp-python provides an API for this). The library
also includes a web server, so you can use llama.cpp-compatible models with any
OpenAI-compatible client. This mode makes local models easy to integrate with an IDE
for code completion and suggestions.
In this section, we’ve assumed the code-generation model we need is available from
the Hugging Face Hub in GGUF format. But what if the model you want is available
only in single or half precision, or it’s available in GGUF but the performance isn’t
great? In those cases, after you’ve downloaded the source model checkpoints and
supporting files locally, you can quantize the model and convert it to GGUF using the
convert_hf_to_gguf.py script in the llama.cpp GitHub repo:
python llama.cpp/convert-hf-to-gguf.py <checkpoints_dir> --outfile
➥<output_file_name>.gguf --outtype <quantization_type>
The script requires the directory for the downloaded model checkpoints and files, a
name for the target GGUF file, and the quantization type (see the llama.cpp docs for
options). You can also upload the resulting GGUF model to the Hugging Face Hub.
After quantization, repeat the steps from earlier in this section to generate code locally.
Summary
¡ Specialized open source code-generation models can match generalist perfor­
mance with fewer parameters.
¡ CodeGen models support multiple programming languages, including Python-
only code generation via the mono family.
¡ Converting code generation models to ONNX can reduce average inference
time by about 19% compared to standard PyTorch implementations.
¡ 8-bit quantization of ONNX models can cut inference time by an additional 60%
without sacrificing quality.

Chapter 8  Generating protein structures
worry—we’ll keep it high level and cover only what you need to follow the model
descriptions and inference optimization strategies we’ll apply.
Chemistry is one of the fields that has benefited most from advances in natural
language processing (NLP). Researchers have reframed many chemistry tasks as text-­
sequence problems. Combined with open datasets, this has sparked a wave of work
starting with clearly defined fundamental challenges. Early models were single-modal,
using molecules as both input and output. More recent work is multimodal, adding
data such as spectra from analytical techniques and human language (such as synthesis
procedures) to bridge the gap between chemical and natural-language modeling.
Some chemistry terms
Amino acid—Organic molecule used by living organisms to build proteins
Antibody—Immune-system protein that helps fight pathogens such as bacteria and
viruses
Oligomer—Molecule made of a small number of repeating units called monomers
Protein—Molecule made of amino acids that supports growth, tissue repair, and
other body functions
Reactant—Substance that is changed or consumed in a chemical reaction
Reagent—Substance added to trigger a reaction or test for one (or for a specific
chemical)
SMILES—The Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System, a chemical notation for
representing molecular structures in computer-readable form (https://biocyc.org/
help.html?object=smiles)
One early and notable effort is the Molecular Transformer (https://pubs.acs.org/
doi/10.1021/acscentsci.9b00576). Organic synthesis is a key building block in medic­
inal chemistry, and a necessary but still unsolved step in synthesis planning is prod­
uct prediction: given reactants and reagents, what will the final products be? In this
work, reaction prediction is treated as machine translation between SMILES strings for
reactants, reagents, and products. The model outperforms earlier methods, achieving
top-1 accuracy above 90% on a common benchmark dataset. The Molecular Trans­
former learns correlations between the presence or absence of chemical motifs in the
reactants, reagents, and products in the dataset, and it requires no handcrafted rules.
Drug discovery is the area where adopting language models has delivered the biggest
gains so far. As mentioned in chapter 1, because they’re trained mostly on data scraped
from the web, large commercial language models underperform on tasks that require
specialized knowledge—knowledge that typically requires domain-specific, often
proprietary data that isn’t available to tech companies. In other cases, a model needs
task-specific tuning, or the data’s structure is too complex for large general-purpose

models to be useful. In all these scenarios, the closed nature of large commercial mod­
els and the high cost of fine-tuning them make it impossible to achieve the performance
needed for drug discovery.
For these reasons, academia and industry have turned to smaller open source pre­
trained language models. These models provide full control and make it possible to
release production-ready models for a diverse set of drug discovery tasks. Each month
brings new specialized models, many under permissive open source licenses that often
cover not only the source code and model checkpoints, but also the training and test
datasets. I maintain a GitHub repo that tracks major fully open source initiatives in this
area (https://github.com/virtualramblas/awesome-deep-learning-4-life-sciences).
This chapter will look at notable examples of domain-specific SLMs for protein and
crystal structure generation, along with ML/AI engineering considerations and sugges­
tions for improving inference performance.
8.2
From natural language to protein structures
The first SLM we’ll explore is ProtGPT2 (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467
-022-32007-7), a model that “speaks” the protein language and can be used for novel
protein design and engineering. Sequences generated by ProtGPT2 preserve key fea­
tures of natural proteins (amino acid propensities, secondary structure content, and
globularity) while exploring previously unseen regions of protein space.
ProtGPT2 is a decoder-only GPT-2 model with 738 million parameters. It was pre­
trained in a self-supervised fashion to predict the next token (oligomer) in a sequence,
using 87,162 raw protein sequences from the UniRef50 database (https://www.uniprot
.org/help/uniref) and without including the corresponding annotations. The pre­
processed training set is available on the Hugging Face Hub (https://huggingface
.co/datasets/nferruz/UR50_2021_04). Given a natural-language prompt, it can gen­
erate protein sequences. The pretrained model is available on the Hugging Face Hub
(https://huggingface.co/nferruz/ProtGPT2).
Let’s look at how this model works and use it to generate de novo proteins in a zero-
shot setting. A companion Colab notebook is provided for this example. Because the
model is available on the Hugging Face Hub, we’ll use the Transformers library to
download it and set up an inference pipeline:
from transformers import pipeline
protgpt2 = pipeline('text-generation', model="nferruz/ProtGPT2")
After downloading the model, we can use the preceding pipeline to generate protein
sequences:
sequences = protgpt2("<|endoftext|>", max_length=100,
                    do_sample=True, top_k=950,
                                   repetition_penalty=1.2,
                    num_return_sequences=10,
                                   eos_token_id=0)

8.3
Antibody generation with an SLM
Our second SLM in this chapter is the Antibody Generator (also referred to as
Antibody­GPT), a specialized protein generation model for creating therapeutic anti­
body sequences for use in immunology, vaccine development, and medical treatments.
Antibodies are proteins that protect us when a foreign substance (called an antigen)
enters the body. Produced by the immune system, antibodies bind to these substances
to help eliminate them. The Antibody Generator is based on ProGen2, an advanced
language model developed by Salesforce and trained on more than 280 million pro­
tein sequences–it was introduced in the paper “ProGen2: Exploring the Boundaries of
Protein Language Models” (https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.13517).
The ProGen2 family follows a decoder-only architecture and includes four model
sizes: small (151 million parameters), medium (765 million parameters), large (2.7 bil­
lion parameters), and extra-large (6.4 billion parameters). The Antibody Generator
models were built using the ProGen2 small, medium, and large variants as a baseline
and were fine-tuned on 5,000 experimentally resolved crystal structures of antibodies
and their antigens (see figure 8.1). All three Antibody Generator model options are
available on the Hugging Face Hub.
Let’s run inference with AntibodyGPT, starting with the small model. A companion
Colab notebook is provided for this example, and it requires GPU acceleration.

8.4
From CIF files to crystal structures
The third SLM we’ll explore is CrystaLLM from the “Crystal Structure Generation with
Autoregressive Large Language Modeling” paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.04340).
It’s a Transformer-based, decoder-only LLM built to generate crystal structures. Pre­
viously, crystal structure-prediction methods—often based on computationally inten­
sive ab initio techniques—typically relied on dedicated tools to optimize candidate
structures.
CrystaLLM is the first model trained on textual representations of crystallographic
information files (CIFs), rather than traditional chemical representations. The authors
argue that symbol sequences can represent complex chemical structures and that LLMs
can learn deeper causal relationships beyond simple correlations. Trained on extensive
CIF data, the model can generate physically plausible inorganic crystal structures. The
authors also added Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) and a graph-based neural network
to improve structural sampling.
During training, the model is given token sequences from a corpus of CIF files and
learns to predict the next token. After training, it can generate new CIF files condi­
tioned on a starting token sequence. Generating a CIF file involves repeatedly sampling
tokens from the model, conditioning on the accumulated generated content, until a
terminating condition is reached.
Figure 8.3 (from the previously cited paper) provides a high-level view of CrystaLLM’s
training and inference processes. As you can see, during training, a CIF file is tokenized
into a symbol sequence. The model processes the sequence, and it outputs, for
each input symbol, a probability distribution over the vocabulary. These predicted
distributions are compared with the target distributions (all the probability mass on the
correct next token) using the cross-entropy loss metric. The targets are the input tokens

Once the model is trained, it generates a CIF file from a prompt. The prompt is
built by concatenating the symbol data with the target cell composition, and it’s then
tokenized and fed to the model. At each step, the model samples the next token from
the predicted distribution and appends it to the CIF contents. This repeats until a pre­
defined stopping condition is reached. The model is based on GPT-2; the model defi­
nition, training, and inference code are adapted from Andrej Karpathy’s nanoGPT
repository (https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT).

To set up the environment, we’ll first clone the CrystaLLM GitHub repository:
!git clone https://github.com/lantunes/CrystaLLM.git
%cd CrystaLLM
Next, we’ll make the cloned source code directories part of the Python path:
import sys
import os
sys.path.append('/content/CrystaLLM')
os.environ["PYTHONPATH"] += (":/content/CrystaLLM")
Once you’ve installed the missing requirements, download the pretrained model
weights. Two versions of CrystaLLM are available: small (25 million parameters) and
large (200 million parameters). These weights aren’t available on the Hugging Face
Hub, so download them using the following Python script (here we’re requesting the
small version):
!python bin/download.py crystallm_v1_small.tar.gz
!tar xvf crystallm_v1_small.tar.gz
We’re now ready to use it to generate crystal structures. First, we need to create a
prompt, which in this case is the partial contents of a preprocessed CIF file. Typically,
the prompt contains the cell composition: a formula specifying the total count of each
atom type in the unit cell. For example, we can specify Na2Cl2 (disodium dichloride),
which indicates four atoms in the unit cell, and use the provided make_prompt_file.py
script to prepare and save the prompt for later use:
!python bin/make_prompt_file.py Na2Cl2 my_prompt.txt
To prompt the model with a cell composition, the format should use the data_ prefix
and a newline character at the end of the line:
data_<cell_composition>\n
The make_prompt_file.py script handles this formatting convention (and more). In
our example, the model is prompted with data_Na2Cl2\n.

This script takes the following arguments:

¡ start—Either a prompt in the required format or the path to a file containing
the prompt.
¡ num_samples—The number of samples to generate.
¡ top_k—The maximum number of most likely tokens to keep.
¡ max_new_tokens—The maximum number of tokens to generate per sample.
¡ device—Where to offload the model weights: CPU or GPU.
¡ target—Where the generated content should be sent. In our example, it’s file.
Alternatively, it can be console.
These are some other arguments we haven’t used here:
¡ temperature—This has the same meaning as in any Transformer model.
¡ seed—Sets the random seed for reproducibility; defaults to 1,337.
¡ dtype—Model precision; defaults to bfloat16.
¡ compile—Boolean flag indicating whether to compile the model with PyTorch
before CIF generation for faster execution. Defaults to False.

Summary
¡ Chemistry language models use NLP techniques to represent molecular struc­
tures as text sequences for drug discovery.
¡ ProtGPT2 generates protein sequences with a decoder-only GPT-2 model trained
on 87,162 UniRef50 protein sequences.
¡ Protein generation uses endoftext prompts to produce amino acid sequences
that resemble natural proteins.
¡ Perplexity scoring evaluates generated protein sequences, with lower scores indi­
cating higher-quality output.
¡ AntibodyGPT fine-tunes ProGen2 on 5,000 experimentally resolved crystal struc­
tures for generating therapeutic antibodies.
¡ The ProGenForCausalLM class loads ProGen2-based models from custom reposito­
ries and runs inference.
¡ CUDA memory-allocation settings can reduce inference latency by enabling
expandable segments for better memory management.
¡ 8-bit quantization shrinks the AntibodyGPT model from 617 MB to 156 MB and
improves average latency by 40%.
¡ The ANARCI tool validates generated antibody sequences that conform to
known antibody structural patterns.
¡ CrystaLLM generates crystal structures from text representations of crystallo­
graphic information files.
¡ CIF file generation involves tokenizing crystallographic data and using autore­
gressive prediction to complete structures.
¡ Monte Carlo tree search improves sampling quality for generating crystal
structures.
¡ Validating chemical structures requires domain-specific tools rather than stan­
dard text-generation metrics.
¡ Domain-specific models achieve effective results with smaller parameter counts
than generalist language models.
¡ Specialized chemistry models require subject-matter experts to validate biologi­
cal relevance and viability.

This chapter introduces advanced LLM quantization techniques that can help you
run such specialized models efficiently in target environments, balancing quality and
speed. The sections that follow describe these strategies and compare their pros and
cons. You’ll also find detailed code examples and benchmarks.
NOTE  This chapter covers advanced LMM quantization techniques for cases
where the methods in chapter 6 can’t meet performance or compute con­
straints. Before continuing, make sure you understand chapter 6.
9.1
FlexGen
FlexGen is a high-throughput inference engine for running LLMs in situations where
GPU memory is limited. Introduced in the 2023 paper “FlexGen: High-Throughput
Generative Inference of Large Language Models with a Single GPU” (https://arxiv
.org/abs/2303.06865), FlexGen can be configured for different hardware constraints
by pooling memory and compute across the GPU, CPU, and disk. It searches for effi­
cient ways to store and access tensors by solving a linear programming problem, and it
further compresses the weights and attention cache to 4 bits with negligible accuracy
loss. This expands the feasible batch-size range and increases the maximum through­
put for a model. The paper reports substantially higher throughput than with tradi­
tional offloading methods.
To give you an idea of what FlexGen enables, consider a GPT-3–sized model with
175 billion parameters. Using the formula in section 4.2, the VRAM required to load
it is 840 GB in FP32 or 420 GB in FP16. This means that to load the model and make it
available for inference, you’d need, for example, six NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPUs
(see figure 9.1).

FlexGen
Given the price of the hardware, running a single model this way can be very
expensive—­often beyond the budget of small and mid-sized organizations and even
some large non-tech ones. Assume a node with one consumer GPU (16 GB DRAM)
but more RAM and disk space, which are cheaper and more available than GPUs. The
FlexGen linear programming optimizer finds the best way to store and access the mod­
el’s weights, activations, and attention KV cache across the GPU, CPU, and disk. As a
result, parts of the model are offloaded, as shown in figure 9.2 (assuming the model is
loaded in FP16 format). This approach is definitely cheaper than buying or renting six
NVIDIA A100 GPUs.
175B model: 420 GB VRAM → 16 GB VRAM + 200 GB DRAM + 204 GB disk
Cheaper than 6 A100 GPUs!
Figure 9.2  Loading a 175 billion–parameter language model with FlexGen across GPU, CPU, and disk
This kind of offloading lets us deploy a very large model in a hardware-constrained
environment, but it increases latency and reduces throughput. That’s expected: CPUs
and disks are slower than GPUs, and offloading adds extra I/O.
FlexGen goes beyond basic offloading: during generative inference, it decides which
tensors (weights, activations, and KV cache) to offload, where to place them, and when
to move them to improve throughput while keeping I/O efficient. It further boosts
inference performance by compressing both weights and the KV cache to 4 bits with
negligible accuracy loss. This is an extreme example using a very large model—when
you fine-tune a model for domain-specific tasks, you typically won’t reach this size—but
it illustrates the benefits of the FlexGen approach in simple terms.
NOTE  FlexGen supports only NVIDIA GPUs via CUDA and has no plans to
support other vendors’ hardware acceleration.

mentations for Facebook’s OPT (https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.01068) and Galactica

This example, in the accompanying notebook, requires hardware acceleration and

FlexGen. After installing the FlexGen code package (as shown in the notebook), you
can evaluate FlexGen on one of the supported models from the CLI by running the
flex_opt Python script as follows:
python -m flexgen.flex_opt --model facebook/opt-1.3b
In its simplest form, flex_opt expects the model argument, which is the ID of the tar­
get model on the Hugging Face Hub. After downloading the model, the script con­
verts the weights to FlexGen based on the selected model’s configuration, then loads
or offloads its weights, attention cache, and activations to the destination storage (by
default, if you don’t specify otherwise at runtime, everything is loaded to the GPU).
Finally, it runs a small benchmark. The output of the command looks like this:

task with a model that doesn’t fit on your GPU, start by importing the required Flex­
Gen classes (which will be discussed as we use them):
from flexgen.flex_opt import (Policy, OptLM, ExecutionEnv,
➥CompressionConfig, str2bool)
Next, download the target model’s tokenizer from the Hugging Face Hub:
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
model_id = "facebook/opt-6.7b"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id, padding_side="left")
tokenizer.add_bos_token = False
stop = tokenizer("\n").input_ids[0]
Before we initialize the model with FlexGen, we need to set up a few things. First, cre­
ate the execution environment for the converted model using the ExecutionEnv class
and its create method. This method takes the name of the directory where FlexGen
can offload data that shouldn’t go in GPU memory or RAM:
offload_dir = './flexgen_offload'
env = ExecutionEnv.create(offload_dir)

handles both. Here’s how to use it to set up everything we need:
policy = Policy(len(prompts), 1,
                50, 50, 50, 50, 100, 0,
                overlap=True, sep_layer=True, pin_weight=True,
                cpu_cache_compute=True, attn_sparsity=1.0,
                compress_weight=True,
                comp_weight_config=CompressionConfig(
                    num_bits=4, group_size=64,
                    group_dim=0, symmetric=False),
                compress_cache=True,
                comp_cache_config=CompressionConfig(
                    num_bits=4, group_size=64,
                    group_dim=2, symmetric=False)

LLMs prepared for FlexGen are fully supported by the Hugging Face’s Transformers
library. When you’re done generating text completions, you can shut down the execu­
tion environment:
env.close_copy_threads()
FlexGen also supports multiple GPUs, which helps when the model you need to run
might not fit in VRAM on your available hardware.
To support other families of open source LLMs, you can create a new Python script
that follows the structure of flexgen.opt_config.py. In it, specify the target model
architecture configuration, and implement utilities to download its weights from the
Hub.
FlexGen provides advanced offloading and compression out of the box, and it deliv­
ers higher throughput on large batches than other approaches covered so far in this
book, such as Accelerate and DeepSpeed. But it’s optimized for throughput-focused
scenarios (LLM applications running inference on millions of tokens per batch). If
latency is your main KPI, FlexGen isn’t the best way to run a larger model on budget
hardware; you’ll need to consider other optimization options instead.

9.2
SmoothQuant
SmoothQuant is a post-training quantization method that improves LLM efficiency
while preserving accuracy. Traditional quantization methods often focus on weights
and can struggle with activation outliers, especially in larger models. These outliers can
hurt performance after quantization. SmoothQuant (introduced in the paper of the
same name; https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10438) addresses this by enabling 8-bit weight
and activation quantization without additional training. It does so by smoothing activa­
tion outliers via a mathematical transformation, effectively shifting quantization diffi­
culties from activations to weights. This makes it possible to quantize a range of LLM
architectures successfully. According to experiments in the paper, SmoothQuant can
deliver up to 1.56 times speed increases and a 50% reduction in memory usage with
minimal accuracy loss. This can enable the deployment of extremely large models,
potentially even on a single node, depending on the node’s hardware specs. Smooth­
Quant is compatible with the PyTorch framework.
Before going hands-on with SmoothQuant, let’s look at the main quantization chal­
lenge it addresses. The techniques described in chapter 6 work well for LLMs up to about
6 or 7 billion parameters. Beyond that threshold, systematic activation outliers often
appear, which can degrade accuracy after quantization. In section 6.2.2, I introduced
the LLM.int8() technique, which mitigates this problem with a mixed-precision decom­
position (it keeps outliers in FP16 while using INT8 for the remaining activations). This
technique is already integrated into popular Python libraries, including some we use
throughout this book. But for larger models, this decomposition is difficult to imple­
ment efficiently on hardware accelerators. In those cases, it’s better to use a different
training-free quantization scheme that uses INT8 for all compute-intensive operations.
SmoothQuant migrates the quantization difficulty from activations to weights by apply­
ing a mathematically equivalent, per-channel scaling transformation that smooths mag­
nitudes across channels and makes

Let’s look at an example; the complete code is available in a companion Colab note­

and weights while achieving accuracy comparable to FP16 on the same model. Smooth­
Quant has been tested on diverse LLM families, including Llama, OPT, Mistral, Mixtral,
and Falcon. For PyTorch, SmoothQuant provides INT8 inference with CUTLASS INT8
GEMM kernels, wrapped as PyTorch modules in the torch-int (https://github.com/
Guangxuan-Xiao/torch-int) Python package. SmoothQuant has also been integrated
into inference engines such as Intel’s Neural Compressor, NVIDIA’s TensorRT-LLM,
and Amazon SageMaker (we’ll cover LLM inference engines in chapter 11). To keep
the focus on how SmoothQuant works in code, we’ll simulate 8-bit dynamic per-tensor
quantization of weights and activations using FP16. All examples in this section require
hardware acceleration.

opt-2.7b). We’ll start with a model that has fewer than 6 billion parameters to see
whether the SmoothQuant strategy benefits smaller models.

Let’s quantize this model. We’ll use a custom function adapted from the SmoothQuant

Listing 9.1  A custom function to quantize an LLM’s weights and activations to INT8
from transformers.models.opt.modeling_opt import OPTAttention,
➥OPTDecoderLayer, OPTForCausalLM
from smoothquant.fake_quant import W8A8Linear
def quantize_model(model, weight_quant='per_tensor',
➥act_quant='per_tensor', quantize_bmm_input=True):
    for name, m in model.model.named_modules():
        if isinstance(m, OPTDecoderLayer):
            m.fc1 = W8A8Linear.from_float(m.fc1, weight_quant=weight_quant,
                                         ➥act_quant=act_quant)
            m.fc2 = W8A8Linear.from_float(m.fc2, weight_quant=weight_quant,
                                          ➥act_quant=act_quant)
        elif isinstance(m, OPTAttention):
            m.q_proj = W8A8Linear.from_float(
                m.q_proj, weight_quant=weight_quant, act_quant=act_quant,
                                  ➥quantize_output=quantize_bmm_input)
            m.k_proj = W8A8Linear.from_float(
                m.k_proj, weight_quant=weight_quant, act_quant=act_quant,
                                 ➥quantize_output=quantize_bmm_input)
            m.v_proj = W8A8Linear.from_float(
                m.v_proj, weight_quant=weight_quant, act_quant=act_quant,
                                  ➥quantize_output=quantize_bmm_input)
            m.out_proj = W8A8Linear.from_float(m.out_proj,
                     ➥weight_quant=weight_quant, act_quant=act_quant)
    return model
This function replaces the linear layers in self-attention and activation with Smooth­
Quant’s W8A8 (8-bit weight, 8-bit activation) implementation.

9.3
BitNet
BitNet is a scalable 1-bit Transformer architecture designed to reduce the cost and
energy use of large language models. It replaces traditional linear layers with a com­
ponent called BitLinear, which allows the training of 1-bit weights from scratch. Exper­
imental findings indicate that BitNet, proposed for the first time in “BitNet: Scaling
1-bit Transformers for Large Language Models” (https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11453),
shows competitive language-modeling performance with much lower memory use and
energy consumption than leading 8-bit quantization methods and FP16 transformer
benchmarks. BitNet preserves high precision for optimizer states and gradients to
maintain training stability, and it scales to larger models, adhering to a scaling law like
full-precision transformers. The paper also describes group quantization for model
parallelism, improving efficiency without additional communication overhead. Over­
all, BitNet has the potential to lower inference costs and improve performance, mak­
ing it a promising alternative to other quantization methods.
Figure 9.4, from the original BitNet paper, shows the BitLinear component (left)
and the BitNet architecture (right), which uses BitLinear in the attention layers. As you
can see, the BitNet architecture has the same layout as a transformer. The main differ­
ence is that it uses BitLinear in the attention layers instead of matrix multiplication. This
binarizes the attention weights (1-bit), while the rest of the model uses higher precision
(8-bit). This reduces computational costs while preserving precision for the input/out­
put embeddings, since the model still uses high-precision probabilities for sampling.
The BitNet paper also reports on several comparison experiments. Figure 9.5 com­
pares the scaling curves of BitNet and FP16 transformers.
For smaller models, traditional FP16 transformers achieve lower loss than BitNet. As
model size increases, the gap narrows: the loss delta is already small at around 30 billion
parameters and drops to 0.09 near 100 billion.

The BitNet paper also reports on several comparison experiments. Figure 9.5 com­
pares the scaling curves of BitNet and FP16 transformers.
For smaller models, traditional FP16 transformers achieve lower loss than BitNet. As
model size increases, the gap narrows: the loss delta is already small at around 30 billion
parameters and drops to 0.09 near 100 billion.

The biggest challenge in training low-bit transformers is optimization stability. The
paper’s authors tested both BitNet and an FP16 baseline by training a series of models
with varying peak learning rates. Figure 9.6 shows the results.
On the left of figure 9.6, BitNet converges with a high learning rate, whereas FP16
transformers fail to converge, indicating better training stability. On the right, BitNet
converges when training with different learning rates—its perplexity improves as the
learning rate increases.

9.4
BitNet and Python
The BitNet framework is based on llama.cpp (introduced in chapter 6), and its core
is implemented in C++. It provides optimized kernels for fast, energy-efficient, lossless
inference for 1-bit models on CPUs. It doesn’t yet support GPUs, but that’s planned.
You can install BitNet from source; follow the instructions for your OS in the official
Microsoft GitHub repository (https://github.com/microsoft/BitNet).
BitNet also provides Python bindings, so you can run inference in Python on BitNet-­
quantized models hosted on the Hugging Face Hub. The main Python script, run_
inference.py, uses the following syntax:
python run_inference.py -m models/
➥Falcon3-7B-Instruct-1.58bit/ggml-model-i2_s.gguf -p "You are a helpful
➥assistant" -cnv
In its basic form, it takes as arguments the ID of the target model in the Hugging Face
Hub, a prompt, and a flag to enable or disable chat mode (valid for instructed models
only). You can also pass other arguments to set the temperature, the maximum num­
ber of tokens to generate, the number of threads to use, and the prompt context size.
At the time of writing, BitNet supports its native models (0.7B and 3.3B parameters)
and the Llama and Falcon families. If you’d rather not use C++ and port pretrained
models yourself, you can use a full Python alternative: a PyTorch port with CUDA sup­
port. The source code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/kyegomez/BitNet.
It’s also available on PyPI and can be installed from there:
pip install bitnet

Chapter 9  Advanced quantization techniques
This package provides PyTorch implementations of BitLinear, the BitNet Transformer,
and BitNet Attention and FeedForward.
With this API, you can create a simple BitNet Transformer as follows:
from bitnet import BitNetTransformer
bitnet = BitNetTransformer(
    num_tokens=20000,
    dim=1024,
    depth=6,
    heads=8,
    ff_mult=4,
)
We use the BitNetTransformer class and specify the number of unique input tokens,
the embedding dimension, the number of layers and attention heads, and the feed-­
forward hidden-dimension multiplier. The resulting model architecture follows:
BitNetTransformer(
  (emb): Embedding(20000, 1024)
  (transformer): Transformer(
    (layers): ModuleList(
      (0-5): 6 x BitMGQA(
        (q_proj): BitLinear(in_features=1024, out_features=1024, bias=True)
        (k_proj): BitLinear(in_features=1024, out_features=512, bias=True)
        (v_proj): BitLinear(in_features=1024, out_features=512, bias=True)
        (norm): LayerNorm((512,), eps=1e-05, elementwise_affine=True)
        (out_proj): BitLinear(in_features=512, out_features=1024, bias=True)
      )
    )
    (ffn_layers): ModuleList(
      (0-5): 6 x BitFeedForward(
        (ff): Sequential(
          (0): Sequential(
            (0): BitLinear(in_features=1024, out_features=4096, bias=True)
            (1): SiLU()
          )
          (1): LayerNorm((4096,), eps=1e-05, elementwise_affine=True)
          (2): Dropout(p=0.1, inplace=False)
          (3): BitLinear(in_features=4096, out_features=1024, bias=True)
        )
      )
    )
  )
  (to_logits): Sequential(
    (0): RMSNorm()
    (1): Linear(in_features=1024, out_features=20000, bias=True)
  )
)
We can easily identify all the PyTorch implementations provided by this package.

from transformers import pipeline
pipe = pipeline(
    "text-generation",
    model=model,
    tokenizer=tokenizer,
)
sequences = pipe("<|endoftext|>",
                 max_length=100,

The Python BitNet package also provides a drop-in replacement for PyTorch models:
import torch
from torch import nn
from bitnet import replace_linears_in_pytorch_model
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(10, 20),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(20, 30),
)
replace_linears_in_pytorch_model(model)
In the preceding example, all the PyTorch linear layers have been replaced with BitNet
linear layers.
It is also possible to run inference with existing PyTorch checkpoints:
from bitnet import BitNetInference
bitnet = BitNetInference()
bitnet.load_model("../model_checkpoint.pth")
output_str = bitnet.generate("The dog jumped over the ", 512)
BitNet could be a viable alternative to other quantization strategies when there are
computational or sustainability constraints.
This concludes our look at advanced model-quantization techniques. For many pro­
duction use cases with local small language models, traditional quantization methods
are a good fit. But for niche tasks involving more complex, unstructured content, you
may want to use one of these advanced strategies.

Summary
Summary
¡ FlexGen distributes model weights, activations, and the attention cache across
the GPU, CPU, and disk, enabling large-model inference on limited hardware.
¡ FlexGen uses linear programming to find efficient patterns for storing and
accessing tensors across different storage types.
¡ FlexGen compresses weights and the attention cache to 4 bits, increasing
throughput with minimal accuracy loss.
¡ In FlexGen, the Policy class sets offloading percentages and compression for
weights, cache, and activations.
¡ FlexGen prioritizes throughput over latency, making it best for batch processing
with millions of tokens.
¡ SmoothQuant addresses activation outliers in large language models by shifting
the hard part of quantization from activations to weights.
¡ SmoothQuant uses mathematical transformations to smooth activation magni­
tudes across channels before quantization.
¡ Models larger than 6 to 7 billion parameters develop systematic activation outli­
ers that degrade quantization performance.
¡ SmoothQuant preserves accuracy when 8-bit quantizing weights and activations
in large models.
¡ SmoothQuant replaces standard linear layers to enable 8-bit weight and activa­
tion quantization.
¡ BitNet introduces BitLinear components that replace traditional linear layers
with 1-bit weights.
¡ BitNet keeps optimizer states and gradients in high precision while using 1-bit
weights in its attention layers.
¡ BitLinear components cut computational costs while preserving precision for
input/output embeddings.
¡ BitNet trains more stably and converges more reliably than traditional FP16
transformers at high learning rates.
¡ BitNet achieves competitive performance while using far less memory and
energy than 8-bit quantization.
¡ Python BitNet implementations offer PyTorch-compatible replacements for lin­
ear layers in existing models.

Chapter 5 introduced the ONNX format and ONNX Runtime capabilities, first in
general and then for LLMs. Chapter 6 covered several approaches, including 8-bit
quantization through the ONNX API. This chapter will explore other ONNX fea­
tures, such as profiling the performance of LLMs ported to ONNX format and tools
you can use to extract useful insights from the profiling data.
10.1	 Profiling ONNX-ported LLMs
The ONNX Runtime (ORT) delivers high performance for running machine learn­
ing (ML) and deep learning (DL) models across a wide range of hardware. Still, to
meet specific key performance indicators (KPIs) for latency, throughput, and mem­
ory use, you may need additional model optimizations and runtime configuration
for a given use case, model, and device.

Profiling ONNX-ported LLMs
The ORT supports in-code performance profiling. It’s disabled by default, but you
can enable it during debugging by setting the enable_profiling option to True in an
ORT inference session:
import onnxruntime as rt
sess_options = rt.SessionOptions()
sess_options.enable_profiling = True
At runtime, ORT generates a JSON file with performance data such as threading and
per-operator latency.
Let’s take a look at what’s in this profiling file, starting with a simple model and then
moving on to LLMs. We’ll reuse the linear regression example from section 5.2:
from onnx import TensorProto
from onnx.helper import (
    make_model, make_node, make_graph,
    make_tensor_value_info)
from onnx.checker import check_model
X = make_tensor_value_info('X', TensorProto.FLOAT, [None, None])
A = make_tensor_value_info('A', TensorProto.FLOAT, [None, None])
B = make_tensor_value_info('B', TensorProto.FLOAT, [None, None])
Y = make_tensor_value_info('Y', TensorProto.FLOAT, [None])
node1 = make_node('MatMul', ['X', 'A'], ['XA'])
node2 = make_node('Add', ['XA', 'B'], ['Y'])
graph = make_graph([node1, node2], 'lr', [X, A, B], [Y])
onnx_model = make_model(graph)
check_model(onnx_model)
To run inference with this model, we need to create an inference session and specify
the execution provider (CPU; no hardware acceleration needed):
from onnxruntime import InferenceSession
sess = InferenceSession(onnx_model.SerializeToString(),
                        providers=["CPUExecutionProvider"])
We’ll test it with three input arrays of random values:
import numpy as np
res = sess.run(None, {
    'X': np.random.randn(2, 2).astype(np.float32),
    'A': nup.random.randn(2, 2).astype(np.float32),
    'B': np.random.randn(2, 2).astype(np.float32)
  }
)

The JSON profiling file contains raw data for an ONNX inference session, broken
down by operator and execution provider. On its own, this data provides little insight,
so you need to aggregate and transform it to understand the model’s performance.
ONNX Runtime includes Ort_perf_view, which reads this profiling JSON file, renders
summarized statistics as treemaps, and computes latency per ONNX operator (for
both CPU and GPU). For small models, such as the linear regressor in this example,
the view is clean (as shown in figure 10.1) because we use only two ONNX operators.

The Ort_perf_view visualizations show one square per operator, labeled with the oper­
ator name and call count for the profiled run. The box size reflects the proportion
of operator calls. For larger models, this view is less useful for performance analysis,
though it still provides a 10,000-foot overview of aggregated operator calls (see figure
10.2).
In figure 10.2, you can see that there are thousands of calls for each operator in the
ONNX graph for the model under test. Clicking an operator’s box expands that section
to show details for each call (input and output values and duration in microseconds), as
shown in figure 10.3.
This visualization isn’t very helpful; it just shows raw data without insights. Let’s
switch to something better.

10.3	 Optimization of ONNX graphs for LLMs
The ORT for Python can evaluate models converted to ONNX—not only the full
graph, but also individual nodes (including custom ones). It can also capture inter­
mediate results within a graph or node. Converting to a new model version or moving
from a Python ML/DL framework to an ONNX graph can introduce inefficiencies,
and evaluating one or more nodes can help you find and fix them.
Let’s first consider the simple linear regression example model from section 10.1. To
evaluate the model’s full ONNX graph, we can use ONNX’s ReferenceEvaluator class:
from onnx.reference import ReferenceEvaluator
sess = ReferenceEvaluator(onnx_model)
We’ll prepare the model’s input arrays as usual:
import numpy as np
x = np.random.randn(4, 2).astype(np.float32)
a = np.random.randn(2, 1).astype(np.float32)
b = np.random.randn(1, 1).astype(np.float32)
feeds = {'X': x, 'A': a, 'B': b}
Then we’ll run the model using the previously created ReferenceEvaluator instance:
evaluation = sess.run(None, feeds)
We can also evaluate a single node in the graph. For the MatMul node in our regression
model, do the following:
node_sess = ReferenceEvaluator(node1)
feeds = {'X': x, 'A': a}
node_evaluation = node_sess.run(None, feeds)
We can enable step-to-step evaluation by setting the verbose argument on a Reference­
Evaluator instance to different levels of verbosity:
sess = ReferenceEvaluator(onnx_model, verbose=verbose)
The verbose argument accepts integer values from 1 (the default, less verbose) to 4
(the most verbose, step-by-step evaluation). For our linear regression model, the fol­
lowing output displays the different verbosity levels:
------ verbose=1
[array([[0.9837985],
       [1.126987 ],
       [0.8049259],
       [1.6867123]], dtype=float32)]

To implement it, you’ll need to modify the original code that builds the model with
ONNX operators:
node0 = make_node('EyeLike', ['A'], ['Eye'])
node1 = make_node('Add', ['A', 'Eye'], ['A1'])
node2 = make_node('MatMul', ['X', 'A1'], ['XA1'])
node3 = make_node('Add', ['XA1', 'B'], ['Y'])
graph = make_graph([node0, node1, node2, node3], 'lr', [X, A, B], [Y])
In this example, we use the EyeLike operator, ONNX’s implementation of the identity
matrix (a square matrix with ones on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere), and
combine the nodes to build the final graph for the updated linear regression formula.
As mentioned earlier in this section, you can also evaluate custom ONNX nodes. For
example, in the following code, we’ll create a custom node that combines the EyeLike
and Add operators and then see whether the model runs more efficiently:
node01 = make_node('AddEyeLike', ['A'], ['A1'], domain='combined')
We can then rebuild the graph:
node2 = make_node('MatMul', ['X', 'A1'], ['XA1'])
node3 = make_node('Add', ['XA1', 'B'], ['Y'])
graph = make_graph([node01, node2, node3], 'lr', [X, A, B], [Y])
Let’s rebuild the model and recheck it:
from onnx.helper import make_opsetid
onnx_optimized_model = make_model(graph, opset_imports=[
    make_opsetid('', 18), make_opsetid('combined', 1)
])
check_model(onnx_optimized_model)
This kind of optimization—combining two operators into a single optimized operator
(AddEyeLike)—is called fusion. To evaluate the custom node (or a model whose graph
includes it), you must implement a custom class, because ReferenceEvaluator natively
supports only built-in ONNX operators. However, it can also accept custom operator
implementations. You can implement custom operators by extending the ONNX OpRun
class and implementing its _run method:
from onnx.reference.op_run import OpRun
class AddEyeLike(OpRun):
    op_domain = "combined"
    def _run(self, X, alpha=1.):
        assert len(X.shape) == 2

ran the benchmarks on a PC with two Intel Core i5-7300U CPUs (2.6 GHz) and 8 GB
of RAM.
In section 5.6.1, I described ONNX Runtime (ORT) optimization levels and how
they apply to LLMs. You also saw that graph optimization can be done offline or inline,
and that ORT provides two optimization sets: basic (including the operator fusion

vLLM
(https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180). The paper introduces PagedAttention, an atten­
tion algorithm that improves memory management for LLMs by addressing issues
of memory fragmentation and redundancy in the key–value (KV) cache. It does this
by storing KV-cache blocks noncontiguously, which increases memory flexibility and
reduces fragmentation—key to improving throughput and batch size in LLM serving
systems. vLLM uses a centralized scheduler and KV-cache manager, similar to a virtual
memory system, and emphasizes batching during autoregressive generation to opti­
mize throughput. The paper critiques existing LLM serving systems for not meeting
LLM-specific needs, and it highlights vLLM’s dynamic memory allocation and block
management as key improvements for efficient memory use in complex applications.
Overall, it is the first effort to focus on serving LLMs specifically, rather than ML mod­
els in general.
The paper notes several inefficiencies and challenges in how earlier systems man­
aged memory:
¡ Contiguous memory allocation—Most systems store a request’s KV cache in contig­
uous memory space. This can cause significant internal and external fragmen­
tation. Internal fragmentation occurs when the actual request is shorter than its
reserved maximum length, leaving unused space. External fragmentation occurs
when different requests reserve different block sizes, leaving gaps that other
requests can’t use.
¡ Preallocation of memory—Existing systems preallocate memory for a request
based on its maximum possible sequence length, regardless of the actual input
or output length. This static allocation wastes memory because reserved space
for future tokens and internal fragmentation goes unused until the request
completes.
¡ Inefficient memory sharing—Advanced decoding algorithms such as parallel sam­
pling and beam search generate multiple outputs per request, but existing sys­
tems can’t share memory because each sequence’s KV cache is stored in its own
contiguous space.
¡ Scheduling and preemption—Existing systems struggle to schedule and preempt
requests because input and output lengths vary. They must decide when to delete
or swap some requests’ KV caches from GPU memory to make room for new
requests or continued generation for existing prompts.
vLLM addresses the memory-management inefficiencies because it limits batch size
and throughput in LLM serving systems.
This paper led to the open source vLLM project, released under the Apache 2.0
license. It’s a community-driven initiative with contributions from both academia and
industry. Today, vLLM is a mature project with the following features and capabilities:
¡ State-of-the-art serving throughput
¡ Efficient management of attention key and value memory through Paged­Attention

11.1.1	 Offline serving
vLLM supports offline and online serving. We’ll first look at offline serving—it’s a
good starting point for getting familiar with the library. A companion Colab notebook
is provided.
In most cases, you can install vLLM as a Python library:
pip install vllm
For supported hardware architectures without a prebuilt wheel, you’ll need to build it
from source. Check the official documentation before installing it in your environment.
In this first example, you’ll get familiar with the main vLLM API in a text-generation
use case. We’ll then build on that with a chat use case and a quantized model. We’ll use
hardware acceleration with an NVIDIA GPU.

You’ll notice that the code for this part is cleaner than the equivalent based on Hug­
ging Face’s Transformers API. The single line that creates the LLM class performs sev­
eral actions (rather than just downloading the model checkpoints):
¡ It downloads the model configuration file.
¡ It analyzes the model configuration and prepares the model setup accordingly.
¡ It downloads the model’s tokenizer.
¡ It downloads the model’s checkpoints.
¡ It loads the checkpoints in the destination device (GPU memory in this example).
¡ It profiles the memory.
¡ It initializes the KV cache.
¡ It warms up the model.
The model is now ready for inference. Because we didn’t specify a task, vLLM defaulted
to generate (it also supports classify, score, reward, and embed), so the selected GPT-2
model is ready to generate text. Provide a prompt, and start text completion with the
generate method:
prompt = "Once upon a time in a land far away"
output = vllm_model.generate(prompt)
print(output[0].outputs[0].text)
The generate method also accepts an argument that specifies the sampling strategy.
vLLM provides SamplingParams, a class for configuring sampling configuration
(temperature, top_p, top_k, and other options supported by libraries such as Hugging
Face’s Transformers):
from vllm import SamplingParams
sampling_params = SamplingParams(temperature=0.1, top_p=0.95)
output = vllm_model.generate(prompt, sampling_params)
This is the simplest, most general way to use vLLM for inference with any of the sup­
ported models. You can see how clean the vLLM API is, which was a design goal for its
authors and maintainers from the start.

11.2	 FastAPI
FastAPI (https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/) is a modern, open source web framework for
building APIs with standard Python type hints. It aims to be performant, easy to use,
and easy to learn. FastAPI is built on Starlette (https://www.starlette.io/) for the web
layer and Pydantic (https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/) for data modeling and vali­
dation. It uses Python’s async features for nonblocking operations and good perfor­
mance under load, and its straightforward syntax helps developers get started quickly.
FastAPI also generates live, interactive API documentation automatically, with either
Swagger UI (https://swagger.io/) or ReDoc (https://github.com/Redocly/redoc) as
the documentation interface (they offer different user experiences for exploring and
testing the same REST API). This documentation is derived from your code and type
hints, making the API easy to understand and test. FastAPI is well suited for data-driven
APIs, microservices, and ML APIs.
Before we serve LLMs with this framework, let’s review the basic FastAPI syntax. After
installing the library, we need to import the main requirement:
from fastapi import FastAPI
Next, we’ll create an instance of the FastAPI app:
app = FastAPI()
Now we can start building routes. Routes define how incoming HTTP requests are
handled. Each route is tied to a URL path and specifies the function that processes the
request. For example, to accept HTTP GET requests, we’ll define a function and deco­
rate it with the FastAPI get annotation:
@app.get("/")
def read_root():
    return {"Hello": "Friend"}
To accept HTTP POST requests, we can define a custom function and decorate it with
FastAPI’s post annotation:
from typing import Union
@app.post("/items/")
async def create_item(item_id: int, q: Union[str, None] = None):
    return {"item_id": item_id, "q": q}
Now we can start the web server from the CLI:
fastapi <environment> <python_web_app_name>.py
Here <environment> can take the values dev (for development/testing) or run (for pro­
duction). After the server starts, the implemented APIs are available at the hostname

from pydantic import BaseModel
