You can package FastAPI applications for serving LLMs in Docker containers and
deploy them to container platforms such as Kubernetes or cloud services like AWS and
Azure. For our simple GPT-2 text-generation app, the Dockerfile looks like this:
FROM python:3.10-slim
WORKDIR /fastapi-demo
COPY requirements.txt .
COPY ./src ./src
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "src.main:main", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
In the preceding Dockerfile, we start from an official Python runtime image, set the root
directory in the container, copy in the requirements file and source code, install depen­
dencies, expose the listening port, and start the web server when the container starts.

import timeit
def benchmark_llm(f, name=""):
    for _ in range(10):

    seconds_per_iter = timeit.timeit(f, number=100) / 100
    print(
        f"{name}:",
        f"{seconds_per_iter * 1000:.3f} ms",
    )

11.2.2	 Deploying the best-performing model with FastAPI
To deploy the selected model version behind a FastAPI route, we can follow the usual
pattern for implementing routes in the framework. In addition, we need to implement
a custom function to generate text with the ONNX-optimized GPT-2 small model:
import numpy as np
import torch
from onnxruntime import InferenceSession
async def generate(prompt, max_length, device):
  pt_inputs_base = tokenizer(prompt,
                            max_length=max_length,
                            return_tensors="pt").to(device)
  pt_inputs = tokenizer(prompt,
                        max_length=max_length,
                        return_tensors="pt").to(device)
  ort_inputs = dict(tokenizer(prompt,
                            max_length=max_length,
                            return_tensors="np",
                            return_attention_mask=False))
  ort_inputs['input_ids'] = ort_inputs['input_ids'].astype(np.int32)
  optimized_onnx_path = "gpt2_optimized.onnx"
  providers=["CPUExecutionProvider"]
  optimized_sess = InferenceSession(optimized_onnx_path,
                                  providers=providers)
  logits = optimized_sess.run(None, ort_inputs)
  np_logits = logits[0]
  output = torch.from_numpy(np_logits)
  predicted_ids = np.argmax(output[0], axis=-1)
  return output

and device to use (CPU in our example). In the body of the function, we prepare the
input for the ONNX model, create an ORT inference session, run text generation,
and decode the output to return the generated text in natural language. The generate
function is declared async because, when the model is exposed through a web API,

and device to use (CPU in our example). In the body of the function, we prepare the
input for the ONNX model, create an ORT inference session, run text generation,
and decode the output to return the generated text in natural language. The generate
function is declared async because, when the model is exposed through a web API,
server performance can vary based on factors such as network speed and bandwidth or

the output size (which affects LLM latency). Making the function calls asynchronous
frees the CPU to do other work while inference completes.
On the web app’s side, we first need to create a class to handle the inputs for the gen­
eration. The GenerateRequest class extends Pydantic’s BaseModel class and defines two
fields—the user prompt and the maximum length:
from pydantic import BaseModel
class GenerateRequest(BaseModel):
    prompt: str
    max_length: int = 64
Next, we’ll create the FastAPI app and implement a route that generates a sentence
from a prompt and maximum length:
from fastapi import FastAPI
app = FastAPI()
@app.post("/generate")
async def generate_text(request: GenerateRequest):
    device = "cpu"
    generated_sentence = await generate(request.prompt,
                                        request.max_length,
                                        device)
    return {"Generated sentence = ": generated_sentence}

for most local and cloud deployments. The next sections cover a different scenario:
deploying and serving SLMs on the edge.

We need to install Git LFS (https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs), a Git extension for

several open source communities):
!mkdir -p dist/models

To convert the model’s weights to MLC LLM format, we’ll use the mlc_llm_convert_
weights command. It takes as input the path to the directory where the model weights
have been cloned, the quantization type, the target device (an NVIDIA GPU in our
case), and the output directory that will store the converted weights:
mlc_llm convert_weight ./RedPajama-INCITE-Instruct-3B-v1/ \
    --quantization q4f16_1 \
    --device cuda \
    -o dist/RedPajama-INCITE-Instruct-3B-v1-q4f16_1-MLC
Once the conversion is completed, the next step is to generate the chat configuration
for the selected model. This can be done using mlc_llm_gen_config, another com­
mand file provided by MLC LLM. It expects the path to the directory where you cloned
the model weights (and configuration), the quantization type, the model chat tem­
plate, and the output directory for the generated configuration (the same one used for
the converted model weights):
mlc_llm gen_config ./RedPajama-INCITE-Instruct-3B-v1/ \
    --quantization q4f16_1 --conv-template redpajama_chat \
    -o dist/RedPajama-INCITE-Instruct-3B-v1-q4f16_1-MLC/

from mlc_llm import MLCEngine
engine = MLCEngine(

You can chat with the model much like you do with the OpenAI API:
response = engine.chat.completions.create(
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the meaning of life?"}],
    model="./dist/RedPajama-INCITE-Instruct-3B-v1-q4f16_1-MLC",
    stream=False,
)
The MLCEngine class can also iterate over streaming responses:
for response in engine.chat.completions.create(
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What's the meaning of life?"}],
    model="./dist/RedPajama-INCITE-Instruct-3B-v1-q4f16_1-MLC",
    stream=False,
):
    print(response)
print("\n")
The MLCEngine class handles only synchronous chat completions. For concurrent, asyn­
chronous generation, use AsyncMLCEngine. If you’ve uploaded a converted, compiled
model to the Hugging Face Hub, these engine classes can download it; just specify the
model location in the following format:
HF://<model_id_in_the_hf_hub>
The chat-completion code for asynchronous generation via AsyncMLCEngine mirrors
that of MLCEngine.
Besides using the Python API and CLI to run ported SLMs and the MLCEngine, you
can also serve them through MLC LLM’s REST API. The server is available automati­
cally after you install MLC LLM. For the ported model in this section’s example, we’ll
start the server from the command line as follows:
mlc_llm serve MODEL --model-lib ./dist

this time, we’ll specify a different action (serve) and provide the compiled model’s loca­
tion with the --model-lib option. The other options for this command are as follows:
¡ --additional-models—Serves multiple models.
¡ --speculative-mode—Specifies whether speculative decoding is enabled (and
which type to use: small draft, eagle, or medusa) or disabled (default).

¡ --allowed-origins—Specifies the allowed origins.
¡ --allowed-methods—Restricts the allowed HTTP methods.

LLM predict multiple future tokens in parallel instead of generating one at a

MLC LLM applications for SLM serving can also be managed as Docker containers

11.4	 Deployment and inference on Android devices
There are several options for deploying private, offline SLMs on Android devices
(https://www.android.com/intl/en_ie/). Many online examples use TensorFlow Lite
or MediaPipe, which require developing SLMs in TensorFlow or converting PyTorch
weights to TensorFlow via ONNX. This section focuses on PyTorch alternatives.
11.4.1	 MLC LLM framework
One option for deploying to Android is to use the MLC LLM framework discussed
in section 11.3. The MLC LLM documentation includes an end-to-end tutorial for
building and deploying apps and SLMs on Android (https://llm.mlc.ai/docs/deploy/
android.html). I won’t repeat the steps here because the linked page explains them
well. Here’s a summary:
1	 Install the prerequisites to build the model and app locally.
2	 Build the runtime and the selected model libraries. This step is the same as for
compiling and building a model for any other destination platform, as detailed
in section 11.3.
3	 Customize and build the template Android app available in the MLC LLM
GitHub repository.
4	 Bundle the app with the model weights.
5	 Install the APK and weights on the target Android phone.
The MLC LLM documentation tutorial uses a Samsung S23 with a Snapdragon 8 Gen
2 chip, but the workflow is the same for other Android devices. Focus on the target
device’s hardware specs, benchmark performance, and optimize the model as needed.
This approach has the advantages of porting and serving an SLM through the MLC
LLM framework, but it also requires installing many third-party, non-Python compo­
nents (Android Studio, rustc, the Java Development Kit, the NDK, and more) in your
development environment, in addition to model conversion and compilation. Let’s
look at some other alternatives.
11.4.2	 MLLM framework
Another potential open source option is mllm (https://ubiquitouslearning.github
.io/mllm_website/), a lightweight, fast LLM engine for mobile and edge devices that
supports text and multimodal inputs. It’s implemented in plain C++ with no depen­
dencies and supports a range of mobile hardware and quantization strategies. At the
time of writing, mllm runs on Android, Linux, and macOS on x86_64 and arm64. You

weights (single-file or sharded). You’ll find it in tools/convertor. Before running it, set
up a Python environment, and install the converter requirements:

You can then use the script for a given model as follows for PyTorch-format checkpoints:
python convert.py --input_model=<model_name>.pth
--output_model=<model_name>.mllm --type=torch
Or like this, for checkpoints in safetensors format:
python convert.py --input_model=<model_name>.safetensors
--output_model=<model_name>.mllm --type=safetensor
Because device memory, storage, and computational resources are often limited, mllm
supports INT4 quantization for mllm models, including custom models converted to
the format this library requires. Only two quantization modes are supported: Q4_0
and Q4_K. After you build the mllm library, the quantize script is available in the bin
directory:
cd ./bin
./quantize <model_name>.mllm model_q4_0.mllm Q4_K
11.4.3	 Hugging Face Transformers
Another alternative, fully Python-based, is to deploy and run SLMs for on-device infer­
ence directly with the Hugging Face Transformers library. This method requires devel­
oper options to be enabled on the target device.
To check if developer options are enabled, open the device’s Settings section, and
confirm that Developer Options appears in the list. If not, go to Settings > About phone
> Software Information, find the phone’s Build Number, and tap it seven times.
Once that’s done, you’ll need to install the Termux app (https://termux.dev/en/)
from the Google Play Store. Termux is an open source terminal emulator for Android
that runs a Debian-based Linux environment. No rooting is required to install it or add
packages through its package manager. Termux is essentially a portable Linux distri­
bution, so you can also install compilers and interpreters for popular programming
languages. This means you can install Python and create virtual environments to run
your own SLMs.
After starting Termux, you can install Python from the command line. First, update
the package list:
pkg update && pkg upgrade
Then proceed with the main installation:
pkg install python

Running LLMs locally can be resource-intensive, so choose a model your Android

performance. The next chapter continues with local SLM deployment and serving,

Chapter 12  Running on your laptop
12.1	 Why use a personal local assistant
Platforms that expose commercial LLMs through a chat interface or API—such as
those from OpenAI, xAI, Anthropic, and Google—can learn about their users in ways
we can’t fully realize. They collect data from user interactions and turn that informa­
tion into assets. Even when platforms let users opt out of data collection or the use of
prompts, generated responses, and other sensitive data for model tuning, their closed
nature makes it hard to know how consistently those choices are honored. This mat­
ters because information can be unintentionally exposed, not only through third-party
chat systems and APIs, but also via client laptops and smartphones connected to the
internet. This is critical not only at the enterprise level, but also for personal use. LLMs
can boost productivity, but privacy and safety concerns can’t be ignored.
Fortunately, as you’ve seen in earlier chapters, there are alternatives to third-party
online models and services, both for individuals who want private AI assistants and for
companies that need secure tools for employees. These alternatives extend beyond
open source small language models; there are also ways to serve models on a user’s lap­
top and higher-level tools to interact with them.
This chapter explores options for running SLMs locally, safely, and offline on a lap­
top using only open source components. This doesn’t just apply to running chatbots
but also to running SLMs for broader tasks, including complex systems such as RAG
applications.
12.2	 Running an LLM locally with Ollama
We’ll start with Ollama (https://ollama.com/), an application based on llama.cpp
(a C/C++ library introduced in chapter 6) that lets you interact with LLMs on your
local computer. You can use any community-created GGUF-format quantized model
available on the Hugging Face Hub (at the time of writing, more than 45,000 are
hosted there). You can also convert your own models to the format Ollama expects, as
explained later in this section. Ollama bundles model weights, configuration, and data
into a single package defined by a Modelfile, and it optimizes setup details, including
GPU usage.
Installing Ollama is straightforward: download the version for your operating sys­
tem (Windows, macOS, or Linux) from the official website. A Docker image, ollama/
ollama, is also available on Docker Hub. Once installed, Ollama exposes an API that
serves the model, so users can interact with it locally, either directly or through a client
application.
To run a model, use the run command in a terminal. If the model isn’t installed
yet, Ollama downloads it first. You can browse the long list of available models on the
Ollama website (see figure 12.1).
The list includes not only text models but also vision, multimodal, and embedding
models. For example, to run the DeepSeek-R1 8B model, use the following command:
ollama run deepseek-r1:8B

POST requests to other endpoints let client applications perform any CLI operation,

served through Ollama:
curl http://localhost:11434/api/chat -d '{

    }

So far, we’ve seen SLMs served through Ollama from the CLI, which is a suitable option
for users with a strong technical background. To make running SLMs locally accessible
to more people, the Ollama open source community has developed an ecosystem of
visual client applications. The official Ollama GitHub repository (https://github.com/
ollama/ollama) maintains an up-to-date list. Which frontend you choose mostly comes
down to preference and requirements.
We’ll look at LocalLLM (https://github.com/qusaismael/localllm), a Python-based
option, which means there’s no need to install and maintain other language compil­
ers, interpreters, or related configuration. LocalLLM is a minimal, user-friendly web
frontend for chatting with local models served through Ollama. It’s built with Flask
(https://github.com/pallets/flask), a lightweight Python web framework. Although it’s
a young project, LocalLLM includes useful features such as switching between local
models in the UI, support for streaming responses, Markdown and code-block render­
ing, and a raw-text debug view (particularly helpful when interacting with models such
as DeepSeek-R1 that use test-time compute). A prerequisite is a local instance of Ollama
serving the SLMs you want to use.
To install LocalLLM, create and activate a Python virtual environment, and then
clone the GitHub repo:
git clone https://github.com/qusaismael/localllm.git
cd localllm

may also want to fine-tune a baseline model on your own private data and make it avail­
able for chat on your laptop or to a broader group in your organization. Through the
llama.cpp library, Ollama can convert custom SLMs to the GGUF format and add them
to a local server for use via the CLI or REST API.
To convert and import a model, first build llama.cpp locally. Clone the official
GitHub repo, and install its requirements:
git clone https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp.git
cd ./llama.cpp
pip install -r requirements.txt
In this example, we assume our custom model is uploaded to the Hugging Face Hub
and under version control. If the model is only local, you can skip the next step. Install
Git LFS, and clone the Hugging Face Hub repo that hosts the model and its associated
files:
cd ..
git lfs install
git clone https://huggingface.co/TechXGenus/starcoder2-3b-instruct
The model in this example is a version of BigCode’s StarCoder2 3B (an SLM special­
ized for code generation), fine-tuned on an additional 0.7 billion high-quality code-­
related tokens.
After cloning it locally, convert the model to GGUF format using convert_hf_to_
gguf.py, a Python script in the llama.cpp source code repository:
mkdir gguf_model
cd ./llama.cpp
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py ../starcoder2-3b-instruct/
➥--outfile ../gguf_model/starcoder2-3b_instruct.gguf
This script takes two arguments: the path to the directory where you cloned the origi­
nal model, and the path and filename for the converted model. After conversion, we
need to create a Modelfile. A Modelfile describes how to deploy the converted custom
model to a local Ollama server and serve it for inference. In this case, our Modelfile
would look like this:
FROM starcoder2-3b_instruct.gguf
PARAMETER num_ctx 4096
TEMPLATE """<|endoftext|>You are an exceptionally intelligent coding
assistant that consistently delivers accurate and reliable responses to user
instructions.
### Instruction
{{ .Prompt }}
### Response
"""

12.2.2	 User privacy in Ollama
Once a model has been downloaded locally, Ollama can run completely offline, so
the user’s laptop doesn’t need to be connected to the internet or a LAN. That’s strong
evidence for privacy preservation. But what happens if you chat locally with an SLM in
Ollama while the hosting laptop is online? Does the Ollama server send any informa­
tion out, and is there anything you should watch for to keep your privacy intact? The
considerations in this section reflect the latest release available when this chapter was
written (0.5.13). Please verify it yourself, since future versions of Ollama may behave
differently.
A review of Ollama’s current source code, along with packet sniffing of a running
local instance, shows nothing suspicious. Everything happens on a locally hosted server.
Still, a few things are worth watching in case they change in the future. The first is
the updater.go file. The body of the IsNewReleaseAvailable function calls the external
endpoint https://ollama.com/api/update every 60 minutes, sending anonymized infor­
mation about the laptop’s operating system, version, and architecture, along with the
current timestamp. This function runs as part of the regular update check to see whether
a new release is available for the local configuration. There seems to be no way to dis­
able this through the local server configuration. The only option is to clone the Ollama
source code repository locally and comment out the following line in lifecycle.go:
StartBackgroundUpdaterChecker(ctx, t.UpdateAvailable)
Then you can build the application locally.
Another thing to pay attention to is the history file. It’s created in your local Ollama
installation directory and is updated with every prompt sent to the local models during
chats. It stores only prompt text, but because prompts may contain sensitive informa­
tion, you should protect this plaintext (not encrypted) file from unauthorized access by
intruders or malware.
You should similarly pay special attention to the Ollama server log file. It’s created
and updated in the logs subdirectory of your local Ollama installation. It records REST

Running an LLM locally with LM Studio
Speculative decoding runs two models side by side: a large target LLM and a smaller,
faster draft model. Both models must use the same tokenizer. The draft model gener­
ates candidate text, and the target model accepts or rejects those tokens to produce
the final output. Because Transformer models can evaluate many tokens at once while
predicting the next one, speculative decoding uses that capability to reduce generation
time while preserving quality.
In LM Studio, speculative decoding works like this:
1	 The draft model runs, quickly predicting the next few tokens as a draft.
2	 The target model confirms or rejects each draft token, accepting only those it
would have generated itself.
This can speed up generation (when enough tokens are accepted) without degrading
quality. But if tokens are often rejected, total generation will likely slow down. Model
choice matters: besides sharing a tokenizer, the draft model should be much smaller
than the target model and from the same family.
Let’s walk through an example of speculative decoding in LM Studio. We’ll use
Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (4-bit quantized) as the target model and Llama 3.2 1B Instruct
(4-bit quantized) as the draft model. If you’ve downloaded them locally (via the lms CLI
or the Mission Control panel in the LM Studio desktop app), you can select them in the
Speculative Decoding panel at the bottom right of the chat view (see figure 12.7).
Figure 12.7  The LM Studio’s Speculative Decoding panel
Once both models have been selected, turn on the Visualize Accepted Draft Tokens
switch in the Speculative Decoding panel to see colored tokens showing whether they
were generated by the draft model or the target model. You can then start a chat as
usual in the user view. The only changes you’ll notice are draft-model tokens high­
lighted in green (see figure 12.8) and faster content generation.

The LM Studio Python SDK
can do programmatically with this SDK. It provides a synchronous convenience API
and a scoped resource API that uses with statements for deterministic cleanup of net­
work resources. The convenience API works well for a CLI or notebook cells. For larger
applications, use the scoped API so context managers reliably close connections and
other allocated resources.
Let’s see how this API works by walking through examples for chat, text completion,
embedding generation, and agentic flow. For the code examples in this section, we’ll
assume an LM Studio API server is running locally and a model is loaded and ready to
accept requests (here, the Llama 3.2 3B Instruct 4-bit quantized version from the LM
Studio online catalog). You can chat with the loaded model using the API with the fol­
lowing very high-level code:
import lmstudio as lms
model = lms.llm('llama-3.2-3b-instruct')
print(model.respond("What is the meaning of life?"))
As you can see, we specified the model ID and then called its respond method. The
returned value is a PredictionResult instance whose content attribute contains the
generated text.
You can do the same through the scoped resource API as follows:
import lmstudio as lms
with lms.Client() as client:
    model = client.llm.model("llama-3.2-3b-instruct")
    result = model.respond("What is the meaning of life?")
    print(result)
Inferencing parameters can be passed to the respond method. Example:
result = model.respond("What is the meaning of life?", config={
    "temperature": 0.2,
    "maxTokens": 200,
})
With either approach, you can stream the chat response by calling respond_stream
instead of respond.

input and predicts the assistant’s response. First, create a chat with an initial system
prompt using the Chat helper class:
chat = lms.Chat("You are a helpful assistant.")
Then, within an infinite while loop, we’ll implement the code that handles chat turns
between the model and a human user.

function that performs some actions, given inputs, and returns a result. For example,
the function could take two floats as input, multiply them, and return the result:
def multiply(a: float, b: float) → float:

We pick up a model available in the local server as usual:
import lmstudio as lms

In the preceding code, we pass a list of tools, so you can provide multiple tool functions

Our example tool is intentionally simple, but a tool function can run any Python code,
including access to the web, local files and applications, and databases. Design tools
defensively: validate inputs, handle failures, and plan for misuse.
An agentic workflow’s performance depends on the model you choose, so evaluate
candidate SLMs (or create evaluation tasks for custom-tuned SLMs) before you make
your final choice. We’ll discuss agentic workflows further in chapters 13 and 14.

12.6	 The Cortex local LLM engine
The Jan application and its built-in API server are powered by Cortex (https://github
.com/janhq/cortex.cpp), an open source local AI engine written in C++. Cortex lets
you switch inference backends (llama.cpp by default, or ONNX Runtime). It supports
GPUs and tries to use one by default when running a model (NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel
are supported). Quantized models are available from the Hugging Face Hub or bun­
dled with Cortex; the supported model list is the same as Jan’s (see https://cortex.so/
models/). Cortex supports multiple quantization modes per model, so several versions
of the same SLM may be available. TypeScript and Python client libraries are in prog­
ress; the Python client isn’t released yet.
You can install the Cortex engine as a standalone local LLM engine or as part of Jan.
After Cortex is installed, use the cortex CLI to start the server:

So far, we’ve looked at strategies for optimizing small language models (SLMs) to
run on available hardware while maintaining acceptable quality. Throughout, we
have focused on a common pattern: an SLM receives a prompt, generates task-­
specific output, and returns a result to the client application or user. This is a fre­
quent scenario, but it’s not the only way to use language models. They often deliver
more business value as part of a larger system.
In this chapter, we’ll explore two popular LLM-based system paradigms: retrieval-­
augmented generation (RAG) and agentic AI. The difference here is that we’ll build
on domain-specific small models only, which offers benefits for privacy, safety, secu­
rity, specificity, and cost savings.

Why LLMs alone aren’t enough
13.1	 Why LLMs alone aren’t enough
In early 2023, large tech organizations started rushing to “win” the LLM race and reach
so-called AGI (artificial general intelligence), fueled by daily hype. That push contin­
ued through 2024 and early 2025 and led to larger and larger language models, based
on the assumption that more data and more compute (and lately also time-scale com­
pute) would make these models reason like humans across a wide range of tasks, rather
than excel at a single narrow task (or a small set), as with today’s ML/AI. The reality
is that, because of their architecture, language models based on Transformer variants
won’t converge to AGI. They are, however, useful for narrow but nontrivial tasks when
tuned on high-quality domain-specific datasets or integrated into a broader system.
For example, imagine we are a Formula 1 racing team. Our goal is to design and
build a car that can compete in the Formula 1 World Championship, win races, and
possibly win the drivers’ or constructors’ title. The engine is a core component, but at
design time, we don’t try to build the best engine possible; we choose the best fit for the
car we have in mind. We need to consider many other factors, such as the mechanical
parts, electronics, and tires, because how well these work together is key to success (see
figure 13.1). We also need to follow the official rules established by the FIA (Fédération
Internationale de l’Automobile) for Formula 1 constructors.

Now think of the engine as a language model and the car as the final system built
around it to meet a business goal. The model takes user inputs through an interface
(web or desktop). Those inputs are often enriched with data from other sources (for
example, a database or document management system) to provide context. The model
then generates content that may need postprocessing with external tools so it can be
formatted and delivered to users or downstream systems. When designing such a sys­
tem, we’ll also consider scalability, reliability, and security. The business value doesn’t
come from the model alone, but from the system as a whole. That’s one reason to
choose smaller models that can be specialized for the goal and work well with the other
components. In many industries, as in Formula 1, real-world tech projects (including
those with ML/AI components) must meet regulations. Compliance is easier when we
control the full stack, including a tailored SLM bundled into the system.
The preceding scenario resonates with professionals in any industry, not just tech­

Combining a domain-specific SLM with RAG
In this scenario, the Formula 1 team focuses only on the engine and may even out­
source its design to an organization that ignores the rest of the car. It delivers a huge,
powerful engine that doesn’t fit, and integration with the other components becomes
a nightmare. This car will not compete for the world championship, and you can’t
blame FIA regulations for the failure. This is what many big tech companies have done
(and are still doing): training ever-larger models, pouring money and compute into a
race toward AGI on the wrong architecture.
Don’t get me wrong: large models work well for general-domain, routine tasks such
as text classification and summarization. But to improve performance, prompt engi­
neering can’t be the only answer. We also need to integrate external knowledge, and
that integration can be costly and difficult because of safety, privacy, security, and other
industry-specific regulations, even for trivial tasks.
13.2	 Combining a domain-specific SLM with RAG
I briefly introduced retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in chapter 2, but in this
section (and the next chapter), we’ll go deeper, looking at it from different angles and
seeing how we can avoid common pitfalls. All the examples in this section will use open
source SLMs for both retrieval and generation.
More than one Python framework is available for implementing RAG. In this first
example, we’ll implement it using specific packages for different tasks (PDF parsing
and content extraction, embedding and generator model handling, vector storage,
etc.) without a dedicated RAG framework, so we can focus on understanding the vari­
ous steps and their challenges. We’ll make things more complex in later examples.
RAG enhances language models by integrating external knowledge bases. Although
large models are powerful, they bring significant cost and integration challenges. SLMs
are a more resource-efficient alternative, especially for industry-specific tasks. In a RAG
system, language models not only generate content but also convert large volumes of
unstructured text and user prompts into embeddings (see figure 13.3). Using smaller
models drastically reduces the cost of these conversions.
In figure 13.3, we can see two phases in a RAG system: offline and online. Offline,
the raw document corpus is chunked into smaller text segments and transformed into
embeddings by an embedding model. Those embeddings are stored in a vector data­
base, with indexes built on top to speed up search. This phase runs when you first set
up the RAG system and whenever documents are added, removed, or updated in the
knowledge base. Online, whenever a user submits a query, the query is embedded and
used to look up semantically similar document chunks in the vector database. The
retrieved chunks add context to the query and are passed to the generator model,
which produces an answer.
Let’s start with a simple use case where we have a single PDF document to query.
To extract content from the PDF, we’ll use PyMuPDF (https://github.com/pymupdf/

as well as analyzing, converting, and manipulating them (recent versions also handle

and content extraction, embedding and generator model handling, vector storage,
etc.) without a dedicated RAG framework, so we can focus on understanding the vari­
ous steps and their challenges. We’ll make things more complex in later examples.
RAG enhances language models by integrating external knowledge bases. Although
large models are powerful, they bring significant cost and integration challenges. SLMs
are a more resource-efficient alternative, especially for industry-specific tasks. In a RAG
system, language models not only generate content but also convert large volumes of
unstructured text and user prompts into embeddings (see figure 13.3). Using smaller
models drastically reduces the cost of these conversions.
In figure 13.3, we can see two phases in a RAG system: offline and online. Offline,
the raw document corpus is chunked into smaller text segments and transformed into
embeddings by an embedding model. Those embeddings are stored in a vector data­
base, with indexes built on top to speed up search. This phase runs when you first set
up the RAG system and whenever documents are added, removed, or updated in the
knowledge base. Online, whenever a user submits a query, the query is embedded and
used to look up semantically similar document chunks in the vector database. The
retrieved chunks add context to the query and are passed to the generator model,

The embedding process (shown  in figure 13.3) uses sentence-transformers (https://
github.com/UKPLab/sentence-transformers/), a Python open source library that
computes dense vector representations for sentences, paragraphs, and images. It pro­
vides BERT-family models (encoder-only Transformer architecture) hosted on the
Hugging Face Hub. The model embeds text into a vector space so that similar texts are
close together, which makes retrieval more efficient using cosine similarity or another
metric.
First, we need to download the chosen embedding model:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
embedding_model = SentenceTransformer(
            model_name_or_path="all-mpnet-base-v2",
            device="cpu")
In this example, we’ve selected all-mpnet-base-v2 (https://huggingface.co/sentence
-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2), a sentence-embedding model that maps sentences
and paragraphs to a 768-dimensional vector space. The model is fine-tuned on a 1B
sentence-pair dataset using a contrastive learning objective for tasks such as cluster­
ing and semantic search. If they aren’t already on disk, the model checkpoints are
downloaded from the Hugging Face Hub and loaded into memory; this code example
doesn’t require hardware acceleration.
NOTE  With contrastive learning, the model is trained to maximize the similar­
ity between positive pairs and minimize it between negative pairs. Positive pairs
are two different views of the same instance, while negative pairs are views from
different instances. This is becoming a new trend for specializing small embed­
ding models used in RAG systems.
Finally, we can apply the model to each chunk to generate embeddings (the embed­
dings block in figure 13.3) and store them under a new dictionary key named
embedding:
embedding_model.to("cpu")
for item in tqdm(pages_and_chunks):
    item["embedding"] = embedding_model.encode(item["sentence_chunk"])
A RAG system typically uses a vector database (the vector store in figure 13.3) to store
and index document embeddings for faster, scalable search. We’ll cover vector storage
later in this section.

We’ll use the all-mpnet-base-v2 embedding model to embed the query in the same
vector space as the document text (see the query embedding block in figure 13.3). We
must embed the prompts with the same model we used to build the knowledge base:
query_embedding = embedding_model.encode(query, convert_to_tensor=True)
Given this query, the ideal results should include information about the blocked
KV-caching strategy described in the original paper. We’ll use similarity search. Unlike
keyword-­based text search, similarity search compares vectors, so the final results
include not only the words in the query string but also other text that matches the
query’s meaning. Both the Sentence Transformers library and the PyTorch framework
include built-in methods for finding similar vectors.
In this example, we’ll use the Sentence Transformers API, since we’re already using
this library for embedding text. The most popular algorithms for this type of search
(also built into most vector databases) are
¡ Dot product—The dot product measures the magnitude and direction between
two vectors. Vectors aligned in direction and magnitude have a higher positive
value, while opposite vectors have a higher negative value.
¡ Cosine similarity—With cosine similarity, vectors are normalized by magnitude,

def prompt_formatter(query: str,

13.3	 Using a vector database
In the previous section, we explored a RAG example in which the knowledge base
was built from a single PDF. In local deployments, where you typically have only a few
documents—represented by at most a few hundred thousand embeddings—it’s fine
to persist the embeddings to disk. But to scale up, you’ll want a vector database (often
called a vector store).
A vector database stores vectors (fixed-length lists of numbers) along with other data.
It typically implements one or more approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms,
enabling you to search with a query vector and retrieve the closest-matching records.
These databases have many applications, but since 2024, they’ve become a key compo­
nent of most RAG systems.

For the examples in this section, we’ll use LanceDB because it’s easy to set up and
maintain locally, and it scales well when you move to a distributed environment. It’s a
serverless vector search database with persistent storage that simplifies retrieval, filter­
ing, and embedding management. It supports vector similarity search, full-text search,
and SQL, with native Python and JavaScript/TypeScript support. It also supports zero-
copy data access and automatic versioning without extra infrastructure, and it inte­
grates with popular LLM frameworks like LangChain and LlamaIndex, as well as data
libraries such as Apache Arrow, pandas, and Polars.
Let’s return to the previous section’s example to see how we can integrate a LanceDB
database into it. First, we’ll install the LanceDB library with pip:
pip install lancedb
We can now create an empty local database instance:
import lancedb
db = lancedb.connect("paperdb")

In the past, dynamic batching, in which a server would wait for multiple
requests to process in phase with each other, was used to improve GPU
utilization. However, this approach has drawbacks, as it typically requires
padding inputs to identical lengths or stalling the system to wait to
construct a larger batch. Recent advancement in large language model (LLM)
inference and serving has been fo- cusing on fine granularity scheduling
and optimizing memory efficiency. For instance, Orca proposes iteration-
level scheduling (also known as continuous batching) which makes distinct
scheduling decisions at each forward pass of the model. This allows
requests to join/leave the batch as needed, eliminating the need for
padding requests thus improving the overall through- put. In addition to
Orca, continuous batching has been implemented in NVIDIA TRT-LLM,
HuggingFace TGI, and vLLM. In current systems, there are two primary
approaches to implement continuous batching. In TGI and vLLM, the
generation phase is preempted to perform prompt processing (called infill
in TGI) before continuing with generation.

important way to use language models, many so-called agentic systems are really just
RPA (robotic process automation) applications that use a model in the usual way: a
prompt goes in, the model generates output, and the rest of the solution consumes it.
In this section, we’ll clarify the topic and cover the basics of building an agent locally
using open source components. Agentic AI is a big subject, so this is a hands-on intro­
duction; we’ll look at more advanced concepts in the next chapter.
A language model, large or small, predicts the most likely next token for a given
prompt. By sampling tokens repeatedly, it can carry on a conversation and handle
many tasks, especially when specialized to a narrow domain with high-quality data. Still,
this approach has limitations. As a chat continues, the model can lose earlier context
because of the limitations of its context window. Language models also often struggle
with tasks such as math (even basic multiplication and division) and logic, which is
expected given how these models work. In addition, because transformers generate the
best next token for the text they are given, if the input has been enriched with outdated
or incorrect context, the output may fit that input perfectly while still being wrong for
the original question. These limitations highlight the need for short- and long-term
memory management, access to external tools, more accurate, up-to-date informa­
tion (including from the web), and ways to break problems into steps and refine initial
answers. This is a scenario that fits the idea of an AI agent.
A software system can be defined as an AI agent when it can autonomously perform
tasks and make decisions on a user’s behalf, using AI to learn, adapt, and pursue
specific goals. An AI agent must be able to reason (analyze the prompt and related
context, if provided, and determine next steps), act (execute tasks by calling exter­
nal tools or APIs), and interact (communicate with other agents or users to solve
problems collaboratively). Agents fall into different categories, but before we get to
that classification, we’ll expand on these capabilities and start implementing our first
agent system.
Imagine asking a specialized language model to plan a weeklong trip from Dublin to
New York. The workflow might look like this:
1	 A user asks the model for a list of accommodation options.
2	 The model returns a list of options (hotels, B&Bs, and short-stay apartments).
3	 The user asks for a list of return flights from Dublin to New York for specific
dates.
4	 The model returns round-trip flight options from Dublin to New York.
5	 The user manages everything using information provided by the model.
Now let’s look at the same scenario in an agentic system:
1	 A user gives the model a trip-planning request prompt (Dublin to New York).
2	 The agent searches various sites for hotels, B&Bs, and short-stay apartment
options in the destination city.

Comparing the two systems highlights the agents’ reasoning, action, and interaction

user prompt to organize a trip), reasoning that breaks the plan into steps, tool selec­
tions (such as a web browser and an online booking system), and actions (using those
tools and their outputs).
Implementing an AI agent doesn’t require coding everything from scratch because
many open-source frameworks are already available. In this section, we’ll use Hugging
Face’s smolagents (https://github.com/huggingface/smolagents). It’s a small library
(just over 1,000 lines of code at the time of writing), and its API is easy to learn and use.
smolagents integrates with other Hugging Face libraries we’ve used in this book,
such as Transformers. It’s not limited to models hosted on the Hugging Face Hub
or Hugging Face endpoints; it also supports OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, and Together
AI endpoints; OpenAI-compatible servers; and LiteLLM and Ollama servers. smol­
agents supports models that handle multiple types of content (text, images, video,
and audio), but we’ll focus on text only. Implemented in Python, smolagents also
integrates easily with other LLM frameworks such as LangChain, LangGraph, and
Anthropic’s MCP.
smolagents comes with two built-in agent implementations: CodeAgent and
­ToolCallingAgent. CodeAgent is the default and is recommended by the framework’s
authors. At each step, it writes and executes Python snippets. By default, execution hap­
pens in your local environment. This is generally safe because the agent can call only
its configured tools plus a predefined set of safe functions from native modules, and
the Python interpreter blocks imports by default except from a safe list. For produc­
tion (anything beyond your laptop or phone), smolagents supports safer execution in
Docker or E2B (https://github.com/e2b-dev) sandboxes.
CodeAgent largely follows the classic ReAct (reasoning and acting) pattern, a frame­
work for building AI agents that interleave reasoning and tool use to execute tasks
(matching the definition of an agent introduced earlier in this section). ReAct agents
use LLMs to analyze problems, choose tools, and iterate toward a solution. In Code­
Agent, the model expresses its actions as Python code snippets.
Figure 13.5 shows the CodeAgent workflow. As you can see, building an agent requires
at least one LLM, a memory manager, and a set of tools.

The HfApiModel class indicates that the LLM is served through a Hugging Face end­
point. We pass the model ID from the Hugging Face Hub and the Hugging Face API
token for authentication. We then define the agent with the CodeAgent class, providing
the model and the list of tools the agent is allowed to use. Setting add_base_tools to
True adds the default toolbox on top of the tools listed in tools.
To start the agent, we call the run method on the CodeAgent instance:
agent.run("<user_task>")
Execution stops if the agent generates code that attempts an illegal operation, tries to
install an unauthorized package, or triggers a Python error.
The framework provides a default toolbox, which we added at initialization using the
add_base_tools argument. It includes the following tools:
¡ DuckDuckGo web search—Performs web searches with DuckDuckGo (https://
duckduckgo.com/).
¡ Google web search—Performs web searches using the Google Search API.
¡ Python code interpreter—Runs LLM-generated Python code in a secure environ­
ment. Add this tool only to the ToolCallingAgent, since code-based agents can
execute Python natively.
¡ Speech-to-text—A Whisper-Turbo–based pipeline that transcribes audio to text.
¡ User input—Asks for user input on a specific question.
¡ Visit web page—Visits a URL and returns the web page content as a Markdown
string.
¡ Final answer—Called by an agent to return the final answer after it completes
planning and execution.
smolagents agents aren’t limited to using the default tool set. You can add new tools
programmatically in two ways. First, you can use the @tool function decorator:
from smolagents import tool
@tool
def find_accomodation_options(query: str):
    ...
You can also implement them as Python classes:
from smolagents import Tool
class FindAccomodationoptionsTool(Tool):

original approach in early LLM-based agents: they were prompted to generate actions
as JSON (or other predefined text formats). The downside is a constrained action
space (the set of predefined tools) and limited flexibility. The paper “Executable Code
Actions Elicit Better LLM Agents” (https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01030) was the first to
propose using executable Python code to unify an agent’s action space. Its experiments
suggest that when agents act by executing interpretable code and collaborate with users
in natural language, they can address these limits and perform better (see figure 13.6,
from the paper). This is a valid reason to follow Hugging Face’s recommendation to use
CodeAgent rather than ToolCallingAgent for your custom agent implementations.

Building an agent
Note that when implementing a local custom agent with smolagents, Transformers­
Model isn’t your only option for loading SLMs. You can also use models hosted on an
Ollama server (covered in chapter 12). The overall workflow is the same.
In our flight-booking example, almost everything stays the same except for the
model serving. First, we install a local Ollama server and start it running:
ollama serve
We can now download a quantized Phi-3 Mini 4K Instruct model:
ollama pull phi3:mini
The only code change required to switch the agent to this model is as follows:
from smolagents import LiteLLMModel
model = LiteLLMModel(
        model_id="phi3:mini",
        api_base="http://localhost:11434",
        api_key="<your-api-key>",
        num_ctx=4096
)
We’ll use the LiteLLMModel class, which requires the model ID from the Ollama
server, the base URL (specifying the correct port if we are not using the default),
the local API key, and the context size. Then we pass this model when creating the
CodeAgent, as usual:
custom_tools = [search_for_flights, find_seat, book_flight_ticket]
agent = CodeAgent(tools=custom_tools, model=model,
                  verbosity_level=2, max_steps=3)
Here are a few best practices for building higher-quality agents with this framework;
many of them apply to agentic AI development in general:
¡ Use only instructed models.
¡ Performance often depends on model size. For agentic API applications, very
small models tend to underperform, unlike what we see in other applications.
That doesn’t mean you can’t use SLMs, but models under 3 billion parameters
may not deliver satisfactory results. Use an evaluation strategy appropriate for
your chosen models.
¡ Keep your agentic AI workflow design as simple as possible to reduce risk, cost,
and latency.
¡ Agentic systems combine deterministic components with probabilistic ones (the
SLMs). Although these models can self-correct, a best practice is to make the
system as deterministic as possible: give the model only tasks it can reliably com­
plete, and shift any deterministic work to other parts of the architecture.

context for a user query, and the other model generates an answer from that context.
This approach works well in many cases, but it can struggle with complex tasks that
require multihop reasoning or connecting information from multiple sources. The
core challenge is that baseline RAG retrieves text by semantic similarity, which does not
reliably surface specific details needed to answer complex questions, especially when
those details are not stated explicitly in the knowledge base. As a result, finding the
right information can be difficult, sometimes leading to costly workarounds, such as
manually creating Q&A pairs for common queries.
One way to address these challenges is to augment RAG retrieval and generation
with knowledge graphs (KGs). A KG is a structured representation of knowledge that
captures entities, their attributes, and the relationships between them. KGs consist of
nodes (entities such as people, places, or concepts) and edges (relationships between
entities), which help machines better represent context and meaning and can improve
search, data integration, and reasoning. This is the definition of GraphRAG.
NOTE  For an in-depth look at knowledge graphs and LLMs, see Knowledge
Graphs and LLMs in Action by Alessandro Negro et al. (2025; https://www
.manning.com/books/knowledge-graphs-and-llms-in-action).
One of the best approaches to implementing GraphRAG comes from Microsoft’s
paper “From Local to Global: A GraphRAG Approach to Query-Focused Summari­
zation” (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.16130). It presents a graph-based approach to
question-answering over private text corpora that scales with both the breadth of user
questions and the amount of source text. It uses an LLM to build a graph index in two
stages:
¡ Derive an entity knowledge graph from the source documents.
¡ Pregenerate community summaries for groups of closely related entities.
Given a question, each community summary is used to generate a partial response;
these partial responses are then summarized into a final response for the user. This
approach, named GraphRAG, substantially improves on a conventional RAG baseline
in both the comprehensiveness and the diversity of generated answers.
Figure 14.1, adapted from the Microsoft paper, shows the general GraphRAG work­
flow. Blocks on the left represent tasks in the indexing phase; blocks on the right
represent tasks in the query phase. Some artifacts (such as graph communities and
community summaries) are generated during indexing but used at query time, which
is why they are shown in a different color. Indexing typically runs offline and produces
a KG on top of the knowledge base. Input documents must be selected and prepro­
cessed outside the indexing pipeline, because the quality of the KG depends on the
quality of the source documents. The extracted text is chunked and sent to an LLM,
which extracts domain-specific entities and relationships (the KG’s nodes and edges)
and then detects and summarizes graph communities. Here, a community is a group
of nodes that are more densely connected to one another than to the rest of the graph.

The generated graph can now be rendered. The visualize_graph_with_plotly func­
tion, which visualizes it using the Plotly API for Python, is available in the notebook.
The indexing isn’t finished yet. We still need to compute the communities in this
graph. NetworkX includes several community-detection algorithms, including the pop­
ular Louvain method. However, the GraphRAG paper reports better results with hier­
archical clustering using the Leiden algorithm (https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.08473),
which NetworkX doesn’t provide out of the box. The reference implementation is
a Python wrapper around the libleidenalg C++ library, so we’ll build a simple pure-­
Python version.
The Louvain algorithm starts from a singleton partition, with each node in its own
community. It then iteratively moves nodes between communities, builds an aggregated
network from the resulting partition, and iterates on the aggregated network until the
quality score no longer improves. According to the Leiden paper, one problem with the
Louvain algorithm is that it can identify communities that are internally disconnected.
The Leiden algorithm is partly based on its predecessor but addresses this issue. Like
Louvain, it starts from a singleton partition and moves nodes between communities to
improve the partition, but it refines the partition before aggregation. An aggregated
network is then created based on the refined partition. The algorithm then repeats the
move and aggregate steps until no further improvement is possible.
The Leiden algorithm optimizes modularity, a metric that measures how strongly a
network divides into clusters. Maximizing modularity helps ensure the communities
that are found are well defined and meaningful. The companion Colab notebook
includes a simple Python implementation, including a utility function that computes
the modularity gain from moving a node to a particular community in the graph:
def calculate_modularity_gain(graph, node, community,
➥ communities, resolution):
  m = graph.number_of_edges()
  k_i = graph.degree(node)
  k_i_in = sum(1 for neighbor in graph.neighbors(node)
  ➥if communities[neighbor] == community)
  sigma_tot = sum(graph.degree(v) for v in graph.nodes
  ➥if communities[v] == community)
  return (k_i_in - k_i * sigma_tot / (2 * m)) * resolution
A higher modularity gain means that moving a node into a community would improve
the graph’s community structure. The resolution argument controls community size
(higher values produce smaller communities). The calculate_modularity_gain func­
tion computes the graph’s total edge count, the input node’s degree (number of con­
nections), the node’s number of connections to other nodes in the input community,
the target community’s total degree for all nodes in the input community, and the
change in modularity if the node is moved. This modularity gain formula compares
the actual number of edges within the community with the expected number if edges
were distributed randomly; the resolution parameter scales the gain.

The goal is to identify groups of nodes (communities) that are more densely con­

function then iterates for the number of steps specified by the max_iterations argu­

gain if the node were moved. If it finds a better community, it moves the node and sets
the improved flag to True. It then runs a second pass across the nodes; any single-node

Once we’ve completed the previous steps, users can start asking questions of our
knowledge base and receive answers generated by the SLM. Global search uses the fol­
lowing workflow:
1	 Intermediate answers are generated for each community summary in relation to
the query.
2	 The final answer is generated by combining the intermediate answers into a con­
cise response.
Let’s see what this implies in code. The notebook’s global search uses two functions:
generate_answers and generate_final_answer. The generate_answers function loops
through the community summaries and, for each one, queries the local model with the
following prompt:
prompt = f"""
        Query: {query}
        Use the following community summary to answer the query:
        {summary}
        Answer:
        """
It returns a list of generated answers for the user’s query and a summary for each commu­
nity (a dictionary whose keys are community IDs and whose values are the intermediate
answers). Downstream, the generate_final_answer function combines those intermedi­
ate answers to enrich the prompt for the local model and produce the final answer:
combined_answers_prompt = "Combine the following answers into a single,
                          ➥ concise response:\n\n"
    for community_id, answer in intermediate_answers.items():
        combined_answers_prompt += f"Community {community_id}: {answer}\n\n"
This is a naive implementation of the GraphRAG paper, and it’s a good way to under­
stand how GraphRAG works and why it can outperform vanilla RAG or other patterns
that rely mostly on embedding similarity. Our custom implementation still has plenty
of room for improvement, especially for local use. Here are some suggestions:
¡ Persist the generated graph elements (entities, entity summaries, communities,
and community summaries) in Parquet format to avoid rerunning the indexing
process for each new query.
¡ Validate the generated entities.
¡ Export the graph as GraphML for visual analysis in a third-party tool.
¡ Rank the generated community summaries, and then filter them by relevance
to the user query before generating intermediate answers. This produces more
accurate answers and fewer calls to the generative model.

14.1.1	 Microsoft’s open source GraphRAG capabilities
As mentioned earlier in this chapter, Microsoft released an open source implemen­
tation based on the GraphRAG paper. In its implementation, it offers two options at
query time:
¡ Global search—Answers to user queries are based on community summaries gen­
erated at indexing time, which is the core idea of the GraphRAG paper. We used
the same strategy in our custom implementation.
¡ Local search—Answers are generated by combining relevant data from an
AI-extracted KG (entities) with text chunks from the source documents
(embeddings). This option also converts the knowledge base to vectors and
stores them in a vector database. This approach is out of scope for this book.
Microsoft’s GraphRAG solution has been implemented in Python using only open
source packages, but it supports only OpenAI’s commercial generative and embedding
models via the OpenAI or Azure OpenAI APIs. It doesn’t support running open source
SLMs locally or using other providers’ APIs. Still, it’s worth considering as an end-to-
end solution: the code is open source, so you can fork the GitHub repository and adapt
it to use local models via the Hugging Face Transformers library, vLLM, or Ollama, or
use open source SLMs through Hugging Face endpoints.
Microsoft’s open source GraphRAG solution includes built-in logic to persist the
graph and related artifacts, such as communities and community summaries. It stores
everything in Parquet format on disk or in Azure Blob Storage or Cosmos DB.
NOTE  Apache Parquet (https://parquet.apache.org/) is an open source,
column-­oriented storage format designed for efficient analytics and large-scale
data processing. It uses compression and encoding to support complex data
structures and fast queries.
Microsoft’s local search option in GraphRAG stores document embeddings in a vector
database. This persistence works out of the box when you use a supported option: the
open source LanceDB (introduced in chapter 13) or the Azure services Cosmos DB and
Azure AI Search. Even if you plan to use only global search, indexing still requires a con­
nection to one of the supported vector databases. To use a different graph store or vector
database, you must fork the GraphRAG GitHub repository and implement it yourself.
Microsoft’s open source GraphRAG comes with a CLI, so we don’t need to write any
Python code (as long as we use only the supported models and storage systems). The
package can be installed as follows:
pip install graphrag
Once that’s done, we can initialize a GraphRAG space using the graphrag command,
providing the path to the workspace root directory:
graphrag init --root <graphrag_space_root_dir>

Microsoft’s open source GraphRAG includes the building blocks, but it lacks capa­

14.1.2	 Evaluation metrics
RAG improves the accuracy of LLM responses. There are many techniques and frame­
works for evaluating LLM outputs (some covered in earlier chapters), but how can we
assess the language models used in a RAG system, including GraphRAG? Which met­
rics should we use?
Traditional metrics, such as BLEU and ROUGE, widely used in NLP, often fail to
capture what RAG applications require, such as factual accuracy and context relevance.
BLEU doesn’t account for the context or evidence in the retrieved documents, which
can leave gaps in evaluating factual accuracy, whereas ROUGE emphasizes recall and
largely ignores precision. RAG needs both precision (how much retrieved informa­
tion is relevant) and recall (how much relevant information is retrieved). We therefore
need specialized RAG metrics, including metrics tailored to each phase of the pipeline
(retrieval and generation).
NOTE  BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) is a precision-based met­
ric that evaluates the overlap of sequences of words between the generated
response and a reference response. ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for
Gisting Evaluation) measures the overlap of word sequences and word pairs
between the generated response and reference texts, with a focus on recall.

For retrieval, these are meaningful dedicated evaluation metrics:
¡ Context precision—This measures how precisely the retrieved documents provide
relevant information for a given query.
¡ Context recall—This assesses how well the retrieved documents cover all relevant
aspects of a query.
For answer generation, these are meaningful dedicated evaluation metrics:
¡ Faithfulness—This measures the factual accuracy of a generated response against
the retrieved documents.
¡ Answer relevancy—This assesses how relevant a generated response is to the orig­
inal query.
In theory, you can combine the preceding metrics into an average RAG score. In prac­
tice, you must assign a weight to each score based on its importance in your domain
(see table 14.1).

from smolagents import Tool
class BM25SearchTool(Tool):
    name = "do_bm25_search_on_local_documents"
    description = "Uses text search to retrieve the parts of the
➥ documentation that could be most relevant to answer a query."
    inputs = {
        "query": {
            "type": "string",
            "description": "The search query string."
        },
    }
    output_type = "string"
In addition to extending the smolagents Tool class, we have added the required attri­
butes: name, description, inputs, and output_type. The last two specify the tool’s input
and output types. BM25SearchTool implements the init function to initialize the class
with the knowledge base:
from typing import List
from langchain.docstore.document import Document
def __init__(self, docs: List[Document], **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.docs = docs
The BM25SearchTool class also implements the forward method, which defines what the
agent does when it uses the BM25SearchTool :
from langchain_community.retrievers import BM25Retriever
def forward(self, query: str) -> str:
        retriever = BM25Retriever.from_documents(self.docs, k=3)
        docs = retriever.invoke(query)
        return "\nRetrieved documents:\n" + "".join(
            [f"\n\n===== Document {i} =====\n" + doc.page_content for i,
            ➥ doc in enumerate(docs)]
        )
It uses LangChain’s BM25Retriever to search the document chunks.

The __init__ function initializes LangChain’s EnsembleRetriever, a class that com­

from langchain.retrievers import EnsembleRetriever
def __init__(self, bm25_retriever, semantic_retriever, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self.ensemble_retriever = EnsembleRetriever(
            retrievers=[bm25_retriever, semantic_retriever],
            weights=[0.4, 0.6])

from typing import List
from langchain.schema import Document
def _get_relevant_documents(self, query: str) -> List[Document]:
        query_embedding = self.embeddings.embed_query(query)
        query_embedding = np.array(query_embedding)

14.3	 Long- and short-term memory management
You can further improve the performance of language-model applications—such as
RAG systems, chatbots, and AI agents—by enriching the model’s prompt with context
built from previous interactions with the same user (or session). Retrieving relevant con­
tent from past conversations and prompts, using short- or long-term memory, can nar­
row queries and searches and help models return more fine-grained, accurate answers.
NOTE  Short-term memory tracks the ongoing conversation by maintain­
ing message history within a session. Long-term memory stores user-specific
or application-level data across sessions and is shared across conversational
threads. It can be recalled at any time and in any thread.
This approach can also reduce costs by lowering the number of API calls and gen­
erated tokens. Even GraphRAG systems, which are more accurate than many other
LLM-based solutions by design, can benefit from a memory-management strategy.

package that addresses this need. It supports LLM-based applications that require
memory management, and it’s compatible with models behind the OpenAI and Azure
OpenAI APIs, models available through the OpenRouter commercial API, and local
open source SLMs available through the Ollama API.
Notable features that make Memoripy stand out include
¡ Short- and long-term memory management—Based on relevance to the current user
conversation.
¡ Contextual retrieval—Memory retrieval is based on embeddings, concepts, and
past interactions.
¡ Concept extraction and embeddings—It uses language models to extract concepts
and generate embeddings.
¡ Graph-based associations—It builds a concept graph and uses spreading activation
for relevance-based retrieval.
¡ Hierarchical clustering—Memoripy clusters similar memories into semantic groups
for more contextually relevant retrieval.
¡ Decay and reinforcement—Older memories fade over time, while frequently
accessed memories are reinforced.
NOTE  Spreading activation is a method for searching associative networks,
artificial neural networks, or semantic networks. The search process is initiated
by labeling a set of source nodes (concepts) with weights (activation) and then
iteratively propagating (spreading) that activation out to other nodes linked to
the source nodes. It is often applied in information retrieval tasks.
Memoripy provides three built-in options for storing interaction data: in mem­
ory, in JSON files, or in Amazon DynamoDB (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/­
amazondynamodb­/latest/developerguide/Introduction.html). Memory storage is
suitable for development, debugging, and testing. JSON files can be a good option for
local deployments.  DynamoDB is more appropriate for large, distributed deployments.
You can also add other backends by implementing the BaseStorage abstract class.
As you saw in the previous Memoripy feature list, user–model interaction data
(prompts and responses in multi-turn conversations) is organized as a graph, like the
knowledge base in GraphRAG. The graph is built with the NetworkX library (used
earlier in this chapter). Indexes on the memory graph are created with Facebook AI
Similarity Search (FAISS, introduced in chapter 2). Graph creation and updates are
transparent to developers: Memoripy manages them internally, so you can focus on
application-specific requirements rather than low-level processes.
The Memoripy workflow is as follows:
1	 Previous interactions are loaded from the chosen storage option, and memory is
initialized.
2	 Once a new interaction has happened (the user’s prompt and the model’s
response), the system stores it with its embedding and concepts.

mixedbread-ai/mxbai-embed-large-v1) and the Microsoft Phi-3 Mini 4K Instruct model
already pulled and available through the server’s REST API. You can install Memoripy
from PyPI, or clone the GitHub repository and install the requirements to get the latest

There are two sections: one for short-term memory and one for long-term memory.
In the preceding example, the long-term memory section is empty because the file
reflects the model’s first user interaction. When populated, it follows the same schema
as the short-term section:
¡ id—The unique identifier of a memory entry
¡ prompt—The user input
¡ output—The generated response
¡ embedding—The vector corresponding to the response
¡ timestamp—The moment in time the response has been generated
¡ access_count—The number of times this entry has been retrieved for any fur­
ther interaction
¡ concepts—The list of concepts derived from this interaction
¡ decay_factor—A weight used to promote or demote an interaction in time
The library uses timestamp, access_count, and decay_factor for decay and reinforce­
ment, and embedding and concepts to retrieve relevant past interactions.
At the time of writing, Memoripy is a young but powerful Python project for memory
management in LLM-based applications. Keep an eye on the official GitHub repo for
updates.

Test-time compute
allowing it to “think” further and spend more time exploring alternatives before
answering. The idea is especially useful for difficult tasks where even large models can
struggle, such as math, logic, and coding. With TTC, a model can dynamically increase
its “reasoning” time during inference, using search methods such as beam search or
tree-based exploration (like Monte Carlo tree search) to explore multiple candidate
outputs within a compute budget. It can then score those candidates and pick the best
one or even execute generated code and check for errors. The tradeoff is simple: more
“thinking” time can improve accuracy, but it increases compute costs.
Recent commercial models from OpenAI and Anthropic appear to use this
approach: on challenging queries, they pause longer before producing a final response,
likely because they generate multiple candidates and run evaluations to select the best
one. Vendors often market this as “reasoning,” but it is better understood as spending
more compute and time on additional statistical processing. While this will not lead us
to artificial general intelligence, it can improve performance on tasks where a single
static inference pass is not enough.
NOTE  Artificial general intelligence (AGI) is a hypothetical stage in the devel­
opment of machine learning in which a model can match or exceed the cogni­
tive abilities of human beings across any task.
This paradigm offers several potential benefits:
¡ Enhanced accuracy and more reliable answers
¡ Better adaptability to new data and contexts
¡ Reduced overfitting because we rely less on static pretrained knowledge that may
be outdated or biased
However, using this strategy on large commercial models comes with some risks:
¡ Shifting more compute to inference could raise costs for subscribers—the big
companies that own the models and infrastructure can raise fees or change plans
to cover maintenance. We often assume the API is backed by coordinated hard­
ware that lets GPU or TPU capacity scale up and down with demand, but we don’t
actually know because we don’t own that infrastructure.
¡ In closed-source models, the “thinking” steps (or, more accurately, the “refining
process”) are hidden from end users. We cannot access logs showing the model’s
intermediate answers, which search algorithms it used, or what code it generated
for a task. For validation, especially in regulated industries, this poses a signifi­
cant problem.
This is the direction that large commercial models will continue to follow. But what
about SLMs? For domain-specific tasks, small models specialized on domain data or
prompted with up-to-date context (as in a RAG system) can outperform larger models
on the same tasks. Could we implement TTC for these SLMs and further boost perfor­
mance on tasks that require more reasoning? This chapter explores these questions.

15.2	 The OptiLLM inference proxy
OpenAI’s o1, its first reflective GPT model, was previewed in September 2024 and
released to ChatGPT users that December. By then, many commercial LLMs (from
OpenAI and other vendors) and many open source models, large and small, were
widely available, but they relied on static inference. This highlighted the need for a way
to bring TTC to open source models as well.
That need sparked Asankhaya Sharma, a seasoned cybersecurity expert and tech
lead, to create an open source project called OptiLLM (https://github.com/codelion/
optillm). OptiLLM is an OpenAI API–compatible inference-optimizing proxy that
implements several state-of-the-art techniques to improve LLM accuracy and perfor­
mance, especially for coding, logical, and mathematical queries.
NOTE  I’m a contributor to this open source project, but I also use it in real-
world projects, so I have been able to validate the pros and cons of this approach.
The OptiLLM proxy sits between clients and an OpenAI API–compatible service (such
as OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Cerebras, or LiteLLM). As shown in figure 15.1, the high-

as you would for direct calls to the third-party API. The only difference is that
the request can include an extra parameter specifying which algorithm to use to
refine the model’s answers.
¡ The request arrives at the OptiLLM proxy service (layer B in the figure), which
forwards it to the OpenAI API–compatible service (layer C), which performs
static inference.
¡ The proxy iterates for a set number of times, making multiple calls to the service
API and applying the selected algorithm and conditions to the responses from
static inference. It sends the final response to the client application only after the
refinement cycle completes.
OptiLLM also supports local inference. You can load Hugging Face-hosted pretrained
models and LoRA weights directly or run the OptiLLM proxy against an external server
such as llama.cpp or Ollama. However, these servers currently can’t sample multiple
responses from a model, limiting the number of approaches available in OptiLLM out
of the box.

Let’s evaluate a local SLM on a challenging dataset using the AutoThink approach.
The complete code for this example is available in a companion Colab notebook. The
code and chosen model are small enough to run on a VM without hardware accelera­
tion, but using a GPU is recommended to speed up evaluation on the test samples.
AutoThink is a technique introduced in the “AutoThink: Efficient inference for rea­
soning LLMs” paper (https://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5253327) and implemented in
the OptiLLM codebase. It addresses two aspects of efficient reasoning: choosing an
appropriate reasoning budget and steering the model toward more effective reason­
ing paths. To do this, it combines query-complexity classification (an adaptive classifier
decides whether a query needs high- or low-complexity reasoning) with steering-vector
guidance (activation-based steering vectors guide the model’s reasoning). AutoThink
runs in two phases, preprocessing and inference, as shown in figure 15.2 (from the orig­
inal paper).
In preprocessing, OptiLLM collects a dataset of query-response pairs, searches to iden­
tify pivotal tokens that affect reasoning quality, derives vectors from those tokens, and
trains a query-complexity classifier on the calibration dataset. As an OptiLLM user, you
don’t need to manage this step; at inference time, the library automatically downloads
a pretrained classifier from the Hugging Face Hub on the first run. During inference,
the classifier selects an appropriate token budget, control vectors steer decoding toward
effective reasoning paths, and, once the budget is reached, the model generates the final
response. All of these steps are transparent to the ML engineer implementing OptiLLM.
We’ll evaluate the Qwen 2.5 0.5B Instruct model (https://huggingface.co/Qwen/
Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct), available on the Hugging Face Hub. To measure its perfor­
mance with the AutoThink technique, we’ll use a subset of the OptiLLMBench test
split (https://huggingface.co/datasets/codelion/optillmbench). OptiLLMBench com­
bines samples from four datasets to test math and logic reasoning.
