15.3	 SLMs with embedded test-time compute
Reflective models are no longer limited to closed, commercial LLMs. The open source
community has helped bring reasoning capabilities to open models of all sizes. New
frameworks that combine reinforcement learning and process-reward models let
researchers and engineers fine-tune models transparently for domain-specific tasks.
These efforts have further democratized generative AI, enabling smaller organizations
and individuals to innovate without the cost and constraints of proprietary models and
APIs. They have also strengthened community collaboration, accelerating progress.
Here are the most popular and powerful open source SLMs with a thinking mode:
¡ Qwen3 (https://qwen.ai/blog?id=qwen3)—A Qwen-family model developed by
Alibaba Cloud’s Qwen team. It comes in small (0.6B to 32B) and large (235B)
sizes, all available on the Hugging Face Hub.
¡ DeepSeek-R1 (https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1) and DeepSeek-R1-
Zero—The larger model has 671B parameters, and smaller distilled checkpoints
(1.5B to 70B) based on Qwen 2.5 or the Llama 3 series are available on the Hug­
ging Face Hub.
¡ Phi-4 (https://huggingface.co/microsoft/phi-4)—This is the latest in Micro­
soft’s Phi family (at the time of writing). It comes in a single 14B-parameter size
and is trained with a particular focus on math problems.
¡ Open R1 (https://huggingface.co/open-r1)—A Hugging Face and community-­
driven, fully open reproduction of DeepSeek-R1 that lets anyone build the miss­
ing pieces of the R1 pipeline, reproduce it, and build on it.
¡ Marco-o1 (https://github.com/aidc-ai/marco-o1)—Developed by the Marco­
Polo Team, AI Business, at Alibaba International Digital Commerce. It focuses on
domains with standard answers—such as math, physics, and coding (well suited
for reinforcement learning)—and also emphasizes open-ended problems. The
authors have tried to address the question, “Can the o1 model effectively gen­
eralize to broader domains where clear standards are absent and rewards are
challenging to quantify?” Checkpoints of pretrained models are available on the
Hugging Face Hub.
For local use, these open source options are available through Hugging Face’s Trans­
formers library, and most have been quantized and published in GGUF format in the
Ollama model catalog (chapter 12 covers serving GGUF models locally).

To balance the need for simplification in simulation models with the preservation
of critical geometric features, a multi-faceted approach is required. Here are some
strategies that can be employed:
1	 Simplification Criteria: Establish clear criteria for simplification based on the simu­
lation’s goals and the importance of geometric features. For example, critical fea­
tures can be identified for preservation, while non-critical features can be simpli­
fied or omitted.
2	 Feature Preserving Simplification: Use techniques like feature-preserving simplifi­
cation methods that maintain the integrity of critical features during simplification.
These methods involve identifying the most important features and simplifying the
rest while preserving the essential shape and properties.
3	 Error Analysis: Perform a thorough error analysis to quantify the impact of sim­
plification on the simulation results. This will help in understanding the trade-off
between simplification and accuracy. If errors are significant, further simplification
or refinement may be necessary.
4	 Adaptive Simplification: Implement an adaptive simplification approach that
dynamically adjusts the level of detail based on the simulation results. This
can help ensure that the most critical geometric features are preserved while
minimizing computational resources.
5	 Incremental Simplification: Start with a detailed simulation and gradually simplify
it. This allows for a systematic approach to simplification and helps in identifying
which features are truly essential and which can be simplified without significant
impact on the results.
6	 Use of Simplified Models for Early Stages: For early stages of simulation and de­
sign, simplified models can be used to quickly assess the feasibility and perfor­
mance of a design. Detailed models can then be used for more critical stages.
7	 Validate Simplified Models: Validate the simplified models against detailed models
to ensure that the simplified version can accurately predict the performance of the
design. This can help in determining the appropriateness of the simplification.

Chapter 15  Test-time compute and small language models
Summary
¡ Test-time compute refers to computational resources used during inference
when models are exploring multiple solutions before producing final answers.
¡ Test-time compute lets models use search methods like beam search or tree-
based exploration to find optimal solutions within compute limits.
¡ Commercial models from OpenAI and Anthropic use test-time compute to gen­
erate and score multiple candidate outputs before replying.
¡ Test-time compute improves accuracy on complex tasks such as math, logic, and
coding, but it requires more computation.
¡ OptiLLM provides an OpenAI API–compatible inference proxy that adds state-
of-the-art reasoning techniques to existing models.
¡ OptiLLM supports commercial APIs and local inference using Hugging Face
models and LoRA weights.
¡ OptiLLM uses techniques such as Chain-of-Thought reflection, PlanSearch,
Self-Consistency, and Monte Carlo Tree Search to improve reasoning.
¡ AutoThink combines query-complexity classification with steering-vector guid­
ance to set an appropriate reasoning budget for each query.
¡ AutoThink preprocesses data to identify pivotal tokens and train classifiers and
then applies control vectors during inference.
¡ Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1, Phi-4, Open R1, and Marco-o1 are open source small lan­
guage models (SLMs) with test-time compute capabilities.
¡ GRPO is a reinforcement learning (RL) technique that, unlike PPO, eliminates
the need for a value model, reducing compute requirements.
¡ GRPO trains reasoning capabilities on domain-specific data using far less GPU
memory than traditional methods.
¡ The Unsloth library cuts fine-tuning memory use by up to 70% while maintain­
ing accuracy and supporting multiple backends.
¡ Unsloth’s FastLanguageModel enables 4-bit quantization with LoRA for efficient
training on consumer GPUs.
¡ GRPO training requires multiple reward functions for correctness, formatting,
and intermediate output validation.
¡ GRPOConfig and GRPOTrainer in the TRL library provide complete implementa­
tions of GRPO reinforcement learning.
¡ Domain-specific reasoning models can be created by fine-tuning base models on
specialized datasets with GRPO and custom reward functions.
¡ Integrating vLLM with GRPO training speeds up RL generation by about 50%.
¡ Custom reward functions evaluate answer correctness, XML formatting compli­
ance, and adherence to the required response structure.
